I beg to move:
That a special committee of five members be appointed, composed of Messrs. Guthrie, Sproule, McIntyre (Perth), Haggart (Lanark), and Ethier, to consider the recommendations contained in the fourteenth report of the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, to amend rule 87 and 88 of this House, and that the said report be referred to the said committee.
The suggestions made by the Railway Committee are somewhat technical, referring to the practice on private Bills. They call for an amendment to the rules, and I think it better to have them considered by a special committee.

maintopic: TERM OF OFFICE OF HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL.
speechtext: As we approach the end of the session I have been asked by a number of hon. gentlemen if it was not the intention to have parliament pass an address to His Excellency Earl Grey and Her Excellency Countess Grey in recognition of their services to Canada and the manner in which they have discharged their official duties. I am happy to say there is no occasion for such an address because the term of His Excellency as Governor General will not come to an end this year.

Mr. McCarthy. I desire to call the attention of the government, and particularly of the Minister of Labour, to the serious conditions which are being created in the west by reason of the coal strike. I would refer him to an article in the Lethbridge ' Daily Herald.'
The hon. member can only put a question at this stage.

I shall simply read this article and ask a question of the minister. The article is as follows:
The closing of the Taber mines brings Alberta face to face with a practical tie-up of every domestic coal-producing mine in the southern part of the province. If the situation is allowed to continue without any effort at settlement, Lethbridge and Alberta will be hit hard. Industries may be compelled to Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
close down for lack of coal and citizens will not be able to secure fuel except at famine prices. Farming operations will be given a serious setback, as the absence of a supply of cheap fuel will put the steam ploughs out of commission, and thousands of acres of land that would have been broken will be left untouched.	.
The Minister of Labour ought to get his Conciliation Act into operation. It is his duty to see that its provisions are enforced. If he allows the Act to become a dead letter in this trouble, he might as well expect it to be a deadTetter for all time to come.
Has the minister seen this article and what does he intend to do to bring the Act into operation? I express no opinion on the merits of the claims of the operators and miners.

I have not read the article referred to. As to the situation in the west, the latest reports received by the Department of Labour are of a favourable nature. I communicated on Saturday to my friend the member for Leeds (Mr. G. Taylor) the statement sent me by the deputy minister, and I have nothing to take back from that statement. We expect that within a few days a board will be constituted and that there will be no necessity to prosecute those who have defied the law.

I wish to add to what has been said by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. McCarthy) that a serious condition has been created on the prairies owing to this strike. From the prairies come reports that coal is very short, that steam ploughs are without coal and that it is feared the seeding operations will be greatly delayed in consequence. I would urge the minister to make inquiries in regard to this serious situation.
House again in committee on Bill (No. 34) to incorporate the Ontario and Michigan Power Company.-Mr. Conmee.

Immediately after the discussion of this Bill in the House the other day I forwarded a copy of the original Bill -the correct copy together with the proposed amendments, to the Premier of Ontario. I have before me a letter acknowledging receipt and pointing out that this is a matter that ought not to be dealt with by this House but one coming within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Ontario legislature. The power question is very important in Ontario to-day; the development of power at Niagara and the outcome of the varied works now being undertaken are being watched with great interest by the people of the province. My hon. friend who

introduced the Bill is well aware that matters of this kind properly come within the jurisdiction of the legislature of Ontario as he has had similar measures before that body when a member of it. He is also familiar with the feelings of the people of the province upon matters of this kind. I am sure the people of Ontario will be very much disappointed if this charter is granted, and I will be surprised if the Ontario members of this Cabinet consent to legislation of this kind passing the House. I need not discuss the reasons for opposing this measure as they have been fully discussed in the committee both this session and last. It is true that the Bill has been greatly modified. Originally the Bill declared that this was a work for the general advantage of Canada but it is not now so wide in its scope. Still I do not think this House should interfere in this matter. There are no just provisions in the Bill that could not be dealt with and dealt with more effectively by the Ontario legislature. I think it the duty of the House and the committee to refuse my hon. friend's Bill. Of course I have no feeling against my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) for introducing such a Bill, my only point being that it is purely a matter for the Ontario legislature and that it should be dealt with by them.

I have no doubt my hon. friend has the letter to which he refers, but I would point out to the committee that because the hon. gentleman has written a letter which has drawn an answer from the Premier of Ontario adverse to the Bill, that is no reason why this House should consider the matter from that standpoint.
My letter was a plain, simple letter without any comment

I have no doubt about that.
Mr. BLAIN

without any comment at
all, and I would be quite willing to have my hon. friend write the Premier of Ontario for a copy of the letter.

registrar of Port Arthur was purchased in 1856, when there was no regulation as to the area that might be taken, and this location is, I believe, about six miles square. This is the answer from Toronto:
Stewart patent dated September 13, 1856. No reservation at all except five per cent for roads. Conveyance includes land to water's edge. No chain reserve.
Who were the telegrams from?
The first telegram was from .T. M. Munroe, registrar of Port Arthur and the second from Mr. Hunt, of Toronto.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the Crown has a right to lay out five per cent reserve as a chain reserve along the water's edge or otherwise?

I do not happen to know that. If my hon. friend knows it, I think he has knowledge that nobody else possesses. In the first place, it would be impossible to lay out a road allowance along the Pigeon river, because at that point the river is a cataract passing between two walls of rock. That was undertaken by Mr. Mowat in the case of the Kakabeka Falls Power Company. He refused to allow the company to go on because of that five per cent reservation, claiming that he could do as the hon. member suggests, take possession of the land adjoining the water's edge, and thereby become the riparian owner of the land under the water. But he abandoned that position, finding after looking into the matter that it was not tenable.
Has the Crown not the right, in appropriating that five per cent, to locate it where it desires in the whole area of the grant?

The Crown has a right to lay out that five per cent in roads for public use, and I was just going to explain to my hon. friend that the Crown has exercised that right on the Pigeon river, so that there is no right in the Crown now existing. The circumstances were these. The owner of this location was an American Trust company, for the original owner had passed away, the Pigeon Biver Lumber Company, now the Arrow River and Tributaries Lumber Company were doing business there, and the agent of that company charged $500 a year for tne privilege of using the roadway across this reservation, afterwards raising the price to $1,000 and again to $1,500, and they were getting it; but they wanted $2,000. This rather alarmed the other company, which was an American company, and they began to inquire.
I happened to be the representative in the local legislature at the time and the matter came to my attention. I advised them to refer the case to the government of the day, and ask them to exercise their right of laying out these roads in order that the
Mr. CONiMEE.
public might have the right to travel through this large location, which the reservation in the patent contemplated they should have, and the government did so. The government did so, an inspector was sent up, and two roads were laid out, a road running east and west and a road running north and south. So my hon. friend has not got even that shadow of a pretense to rely on. It has gone, and gone for ever.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he has any other evidence with him of the correctness of the statement he is now making, namely, that the Crown has already appropriated this five per cent and exhausted its right, and that that five per cent is not appropriated along the river banks.

I have made the statement to the House of my own personal knowledge. I was told by the Commissioner of Crown Lands at the time, the Hon. Mr. Gibson, that they could not lay out any more roads through the location because they had exhausted the five per cent. I cannot give my hon. friend any better information than that. He will have to take my word for it or doubt it.

Well, the matter rests there. Now the hon. gentleman has said, and correctly, I think, that the Premier of Ontario might regard with suspicion this measure because of the name that was placed upon it in promoting it. I believe in that respect, as in many other respects, the Premier of Ontario would be sustained by the same overwhelming majority he has behind him in other matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman appears to be casting doubt on the words of a member of this House. I may have misunderstood him, but if that was not his intention, then there is no breach of order.

If the hon. gentleman will look at clause 14 of the Bill he will see that if the company gets these powers and uses them, the province and the Dominion will get the development of resources that are now idle, and they will have perpetual control, through their parliament and through their representatives.
This is the first time I have ever heard that public control over a utility brings a compensation to the people as a payment for it, and that is all the public domain has to yield.

There is no public domain. I have just shown that the land has passed out of the hands of the Crown in 1856. Under the patents of that day the right extended to the centre of the stream. If the hon. gentleman will show by some argument of some effect that the province has any right, even a shadow of a right, he would be making some point, which he has not yet done.

The hon. gentleman has not established by any evidence that this part of this river has been granted, i do not understand the hon. gentleman s words even to mean it; because certainly the telegrams he has read contain no such statements. The bed of this Tiver, as are the beds of all the rivers in the province of Ontario, is part of the public lands of the province, and as such is vested in the Crown, in the right of the province, and there has been no grant made of the bed of these rivers, from the statement of the hon. gentleman himself. Then the hon. gentleman says that it is because they are going to export this power that it becomes an international work. It becomes no more an international work than a factory that manufactures furniture, or boots and shoes, or anything else. I cannot see the difference. If it exports power, that is a particular reason why the people of this country 1694
should have some control over it. The Bill has been very much boiled down, and many of the notoriously objectionable features have been removed, but that does not touch the vital point of this Bill. I do not care how the hon. gentleman may pare it down, may take out a river here or a river there, or a power here or a power there to export; the fact remains that the hon. gentleman is seeking to obtain from this parliament a grant of what belongs to the people of the province of Ontario. The hon. gentleman argues that this is an international stream. Now with all due deference to the opinion of hon. gentlemen who differ with me, I venture to say that that does not alter the fact. The British North America Act, by section 109, vested in the province of Ontario, at confederation, all this public domain, with its lands, its minerals, its royalties, its mines, its water and so forth, and part of that public domain is the bed of the rivers, which are public lands.
Does the hon. member contend that the province of Ontario has ownership in the water?

I am dealing with that; I say that all those assets formed part of the public domain at the time of confederation. Now the fact that a river divides two provinces, or divides this country from a neighbouring country, makes no difference in the ownership of the bed of the river. It makes only this difference, that in so far as the waters in rivers are concerned, they are international waters, but the province has the same rights over the Canadian portion of that river as it has over a stream in the highlands of Ontario. The province has to police all those waters, it has to regulate them municipally, and has the same control over them that it has over the inland waters.
I would like the hon. gentleman to say who he thinks owns the title of this Pigeon river. It is evident from these telegrams that the land next to the edge of the stream has been granted.
No.
Yes, that is what the telegram says.

The hon. gentleman knows, and I will accept his word. He is very fair in these matters! as in all matters. The Crown has reserved a five per cent area out of this whole grant. Now the hon. gentleman tells us that he knows that the Crown has exercised a part of that righ1>-I do not understand him to say the whole of it, by opening up highways. Now the Crown may apply or appropriate any right that it likes. The hon. member for Essex knows well that along all the navigable rivers and streams or lakes in the province

of Ontario, the Crown has reserved one chain along the shore.
By general statute?

Yes. 1 will abandon my own argument for a moment and take the hon. gentleman's argument. I will say that the fee of half of the bed of the Pigeon river, that portion which lies in the province, is vested in Ontario. The objection that I am making is that this parliament is attempting to deal with something that belongs exclusively to the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario has asserted its claim. It is to-day, as it were, at the bar of this House claiming that this parliament should not exercise the rights of ownership that the province is lawfully entitled to under the constitution of the country, and appealing to this parliament not to make a grant of a part of the public domain of Ontario, to a band of commercial exploiters who are seeking to obtain, in defiance of the people of Ontario, that which belongs to the people, without paying any compensation therefor. The right hon. gentleman who leads the government, I understand, desires that clause 2 of the Bill should be dropped. That is the clause which declares the work to be for the general advantage of Canada. That very fact is an argument that this is not a Dominion undertaking, but that it is local and provincial in its nature. It is either one thing or the other; it is either a Dominion undertaking or a provincal undertaking. If it is a Dominion undertaking it is proper that it should be dignified as a work for the general advantage of Canada. But, if it is not, that is an argument that the Bill is before the wrong parliament and that the promoters are invoking the wrong jurisdiction. As such I think that logically the whole Bill should fall to the ground. It is shorn of many of its objectionable features because of the abandoning of the Nipigon river from the operation of the Bill. In what way have these rivers been dealt with in the past? Take, for example, the Niagara river, which affords the best precedent and in fact is the only precedent in dealing with international waters. The argument which has been made by those interested in this Bill is that the Pigeon river is navigable and international. The fact that it is navigable in no way vests in this government the fee in the waters or the lands under those waters. So far as navigation and shipping are concerned, under the British North America Act, the right is transferred to this parliament. It has the right to regulate navigation and shipping. That is right, that is admitted and there can be no two opinions about it. Now, we come to deal with the Niagara river. It is navi-

gable from Fort Erie to Chippewa, above the falls, for some distance below the falls and then below that again from Queenston to Niagara-on-the-Lake, and it is international throughout its entire length and divides the province of Ontario and New York state. The first dealing with this water internationally was in 1882, when Lord Dufferin, the then Governor General, conceived the very praiseworthy 'scheme of forming an international park at Niagara Falls.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Perhaps it was 1872. I think my right hon. friend is right in that. At that time Sir Oliver Mowat was the premier of Ontario, and negotiations were carried on between the government of Ontario and the state of New York.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I think the Bill is under discussion. I do not think the hon. gentleman is discussing the Bill before the committee. I do not think the question that the hon. gentleman is discussing is germane to the question. I understand we are discussing the first section of the Bill now.
Before you rule, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am prepared to rule. The question as to the incorporation of this company involves a very broad view and I am not prepared as yet to rule that the hon. gentleman is out of order.

I was just showing the analogy between the dealings of this parliament and the provincial legislature with the Niagara river which is identical in all respects for the purposes of this argument, with the Bill before the, committee. The province of Ontario, Sir Oliver Mowat being the Premier at that time, dealt with the state of New York and legislation of this parliament was not invoked at that time. They dealt with the riparian rights on both sides of the river and formed an international park. That was quite sufficient, and no one ever questioned the right of these parties to deal with that river and to dispose of the lands bordering upon it as they did. In 1892 the Niagara Power Company, then exploiting the power on the American side, came .to this country and sought charter rights to utilize the power of the Niagara Falls on the Canadian side. It was then an experiment and the company,
I presume, felt that if the experiment were successful on the American side they ought to get the benefit of their venture by having certain powers on the Canadian side. At that time the Canadian Niagara Power Company was incorporated by the province of Ontario and eminent counsel both in Ontario and in New York state

passed opinions upon the legality and propriety of its charter rights. The New York state authorities gave the powers on the American side and the province of Ontario gave powers on the Canadian side. The company has been operated from 1892 to the present time under a provincial charter exclusively. That was the pioneer company at the Falls. The Niagara case is exactly similar to that of the Pigeon river. It is an international water and navigable above and below the falls just the same as the Pigeon river. Other companies have sought rights on the Canadian side since then, and I think I am correct in saying that only two companies have been incorporated. One is the Electrical Development Company, of comparatively recent organization, and the other is the Ontario Power Company. What did the companies do when they wanted charter rights? They went to the province of Ontario whenj I think, Sir Oliver Mowat was still premier, and they made a bargain with the province for certain power rights. They entered into a solemn compact and agreement with the province and they legislated in Ontario upon that agreement and legalized it. Then they came down to this parliament and this government and Sir Aemilius Irving, as counsel for the province, came on both occasions and presented to this House and this government the joint agreement of the contracting parties, the Ontario government on one hand and the Power Company on the other. They presented their agreement and jointly asked this parliament to confirm that legislation and agreement. Presumably they came here because they wanted wider powers to help their bonding privileges. Any hon. gentleman can see that it was desirable and wise that they should have the legislation and agreement confirmed so that in case of a difference, or dispute, or disagreement at any future time they would have a tribunal to appeal to that had incorporated them and that was not a party to the bargain. That has been the practice in the past and this is an invasion. I do not see how the promoter can expect to have it carried. He has come to this House attempting to exploit the water-powers of the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario has a policy in regard to water-powers and is exacting royalties, as other provinces are, from those who use these water-powers. The provinces at confederation got little enough; the total budget of Ontario to-day is somewhat less than the budget of the city of Toronto, and I think the same thing applies to the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal. The provinces gave up most of their rights at confederation and I think they are entitled to the few rights they did retain, their rights of property, water-powers, &c.
Other provinces have sold these powers and are to-day deriving revenues from them. What Ontario asks in this respect is that you keep your hands off her.
How would this Bill prevent the province from getting a revenue if it has rights? There is nothing in the Bill to that effect. The province of Ontario has to be applied to and has to agree.
Then why is the hon. gentleman asking for this Bill here?
Because the powers cannot be obtained and the securities be dealt with unless they get Dominion legislation.
To what clause in the Bill is the hon. gentleman referring?
Clause 19. Under that clause the province would have to be paid for any
There is no right of royalty or compensation there.
I beg to differ from the hon. gentleman on that point.
The hon. gentlenjan is mistaken in that. The hon. gentleman said there was a right of royalty reserved in this Bill.
I did not say anything of the kind. I said if the province had rights they had to be paid for.
I accept that, and if they have rights in the water-power and the bed of the river where are they to get compensation for them?
They cannot be taken without payment.
To whom?
To them, to whoever the owners are.
I can hardly believe the hon. gentleman is arguing what he says.

The government has no more powers to take property from a private individual or any one else than a railway company and a railway company cannot take property without paying for it. The hon. gentleman knows that much about the Bill.

The hon. gentleman is asking permission to utilize a waterpower. There is no provision for payment or compensation, direct or indirect. He is asking a perpetual franchise for something which the province is selling in other places, as other provinces are. Thus, although the Bill is whittled down, although it is not as fat a proposition as when it first came before the House, it is no less objectionable now than it was then, in principle and in fact. The hon. gentleman

cannot point to any similar Bill passing this House. If we pass this no part of the public domain of any province is safe, water-power is as much a part of the property of the province of Ontario as the parliament buildings at Toronto, the model farm at Guelph or the timber reserves of the province. The question of value is of no consequence, it is a question of principle because if this parliament arrogates to itself the right to exploit the public domain of any province, it matters not how much you take on the first occasion, you admit the principle and we are told in every committee of this House now as a justification for passing Bills that a similar Bill passed last week, or last month or last session. Precedents are created and are followed, and I suppose that is only right and proper, but I warn the government and this committee against creating this precedent.
The premier of Ontario is as stoutly opposed to this legislation to-day as when the Bill was first brought in, and I ask the right hon. gentleman what compensation this House is going to get from openly defying the express wishes of a province in regard to a matter in which it has an absolute vested right. The government of Ontario sent counsel down to the committee and the matter was argued there. It is true that the committee by a large majority sustained the promoter of the Bill but the majority of that committee was not composed of gentlemen from Ontario. I do not think that this matter has been fairly dealt with. The right hon. gentleman and his ministers were not in that committee but they are here in this committee, in the tribunal to which the province of Ontario now appeals and the facts are before them. The province of Ontario is here at the bar of the House, demanding and asking that this legislation be not passed. They say:	You are
exploiting part of our public domain, of what belongs to the people of Ontario, and vesting it in a band of private exploiters for their own private commercial purposes. Staring that fact in the face, is it right or proper to grant the powers asked for in this Bill? No hon. gentleman can successfully argue that this is not a part of the public domain of Ontario. I trust that the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke) who is a lawyer himself

Will the hon. gentleman say how he distinguishes this from the case of the Winnipeg river at Kenora where it was held that the bed of the river had passed to tne owners of the adjoining property? This case was recently dealt with by the Court of Appeals.
I do not know anything about that case.
That was held to be a navigable river.
Here we are dealing with the case of this parliament giving to a private exploiter something that belongs to a province.
You are assuming that.
I think that in that case it was decided that where the land is granted to the water's edge the owners of that land take the ownership to the centre of the river.
Not necessarily.
That was held in that case.
Granting all he says, what has that to do with water-power which is part of the public property just as timber or mines?
If they own the bed of the river, do they not own the water over it?

No, not necessarily, the Rivers and Streams Bill settled that, and according to the judgment of the Privy Council the water is not vested. The hon. gentleman who is promoting the Bill does not attempt to argue that, he says the waters are vested in the Dominion. The only proper way to dispose of this Bill is to have it withdrawn, and so free this House from the responsibility of raising a question that perhaps cannot be easily set at rest. The hon. gentleman who promotes the Bill says the premier of Ontario has sometimes had his acts disallowed. I would remind the hon. gentleman that the acts of this parliament have sometimes been held to be ultra vires, and I question if this Act is not in its essence ultra vires of the Dowers of this parliament. So why embark on troubled waters of that character? The proper thing to do is to send this Bill to the province of Ontario which is dealing with similar Bills and has the only just right to deal with them.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be allowed to interfere in this debate at this moment to endeavour to ascertain where we are and what are the questions before us. The first question is that of jurisdiction, has this parliament jurisdiction over this Bill or has it not? My hon. friend who has just addressed the House, (Mr. Macdonell), has stated emphatically that in his opinion this parliament has no jurisdiction over the matters which are now before us. I beg to take an altogether different view from my hon. friend and I think that on reflection he will agree that his opinion is erroneous. This Bill seeks to provide for the incorporation of a company to which power is to be given to develop water-power in a navigable stream,

the Pigeon river, which is a part of the boundary line between Canada and the United States. That is what gives jurisdiction to this parliament.
Why does the right hon. gentleman say that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is an international stream. This is a matter on which the Dominion alone has jurisdiction. On all matters of an international character this parliament and not the local legislature has power. The promoter of this Bill has truly stated that this Bill alone will not effect the object sought. Similar legislation must also be obtained from a foreign country. If there is no legislation from the American authorities my hon. friend will be powerless to go on whether he obtains power from this government or the legislature of Ontario, he would have no right to put dams across the river, he must have the joint control of the two legislatures, and this is the reason why this parliament and not the province of Ontario has jurisdiction in this matter. It is an international stream and even if there was a similar jurisdiction in this parliament and in the province of Ontario, for reasons of policy alone this parliament should assume the jurisdiction in all matters in which it is sought to interfere with navigable rivers which are of an international character. The Minister of Justice gave his opinion that we have power to deal with this matter, and for my part I am disposed to agree that not only have we power, but we alone, the parliament of Canada, have the right to legislate in matters of this kind.
That point being granted there was no difficulty in removing the second section of the Bill, which asserted that the works authorized were for the general advantage of Canada. If these words were necessary to give jurisdiction to this parliament, I would be opposed to these words, but in my humble opinion these words are absolutely unnecessary and do not add to the powers that we propose to give, I believe they are a useless encumbrance and I asked my hon. friend to remove them and he has done so.
They do not make any difference if we do pass the Bill?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It does not make any difference whether they are in it or not. My opinion and the opinion of the Minister of Justice is that this parliament has jurisdiction to pass the legislation now before us. I stated on a former occasion that the whole point is on the question of expropriation. There would apparently be no objection to the passage of this Bill if the powers of expropriation were removed. This only strengthens the argument I make, that we are losing time in discussing the provisions of the
Bill which are not essential. We should come at once to the power of expropriation and ascertain whether the powers of expropriation exceed the powers which we are competent to grant. The whole argument of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) has been directed not against the Bill, but against the powers of expropriation, as he says, taking powers from Ontario which belong to it. That will be discussed later on. When the Bill was before us on a former occasion I stated that the position of the government would be that we would not interfere with the legislative powers of the province of Ontario, and acting upon this opinion, expressed by the government, my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) has agreed to remove from the powers of expropriation the Nipigon river and this is satisfactory to the gentlemen opposing the Bill. When we come to discuss the powers of expropriation which still remain on the Pigeon river, I said to my hon. friend, that I for one would reserve an open mind and I would see whether or not we were invading the powers of the province of Ontario. So it seems to me that all the objections of hon. gentlemen opposite will be met if we come at once to the powers of expropriation because that is the only difficulty there is in this Bill, and the clauses relating to expropriation could lie amended or not amended according to their views, that would be a question to be debated later on. At this moment it seems to me we should expedite the business of the House. If we want to secure the blessing of an early prorogation we should come to the real difficulty in the case and not debate what is not in issue.

My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) at a moment when the Prime Minister was engaged,, called the attention of the committee to the fact that he had a communication from the Premier of Ontario. According to the notice of amendments in the Votes and Proceedings, the amended Bill was to come up for the first time to-day, so we could not expect that the Ontario government, having had an intimation as to the position which the government proposed to take when this matter was under discussion on April 19, would be prepared to present its case today for the consideration of the committee. If the rights of the province are to be reasonably safeguarded, it is at least essential that this Bill, being admittedly a measure that may invade provincial rights, the Ontario legislature should at least have an opportunity of presenting its views each time the Bill is presented in an altered form. I understood the position of the right hon. the Prime Minister as enunciated on April 19, in a somewhat broader sense than his suggestion of this morning, and I venture to say that the Ontario government and the members of this House

interpreted it in the same way. I am quite prepared to take the view of the right hon. gentleman, as he suggested this morning, possibly what he meant, but I think the language he used on April 19 is capable of a broader interpretation, and I shall read, the right hon. gentleman's words in order to strengthen my request to him to allow this matter to stand until the province shall be in a position to properly present its views to the members of the House. The right hon. gentleman, on the occasion to which I refer, dealt with the decision of the Minister of Justice and concluded by saying that for his part, the Minister of Justice, having said that this parliament had jurisdiction, he would be prepared to accept the minister's views rather than the views of other gentlemen who had spoken. Then the Tight hon. gentleman continued. I understood at the time, as I think the House did, that that was virtually an end of this matter. That he had come to the conclusion that, although parliament had iurisdiction if it desired to exercise it, he wished the promoter of the Bill to understand that this was a matter of fair regard for the rights and interests of the province, and that the jurisdiction of this parliament was not going to be exercised in this case. This is what the right hon. gentleman said:
But that is not the kernel of the discussion we have had at present. It matters not whether this parliament has jurisdiction, or whether the local legislature has jurisdiction, the point is this: Are there provisions in this Bill which affect the power of the local legislature and the local government? That is the only point which weighs with me. Section 2 of this Bill is a clause with which we are familiar-and it was not invented I may sav to mv hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) by the Liberal party; it is a relic of former days, and, perhaps in the case of this as in the case of other relics, we may be wrong in not doing away with them. At all events, the hon. gentleman and I may agree that it ought to be eliminated from the Bill. But the whole discussion we have heard this afternoon has been directed to one point, and one point alone-and that is that the power of expropriation of water-powers belonging to the local government of Ontario contained in this Bill should be eliminated.
I think if these two sections were amended, there would not be so much objection to the Bill. I would have some abjections to another which I shall come to presently. I was struck by the argument put forward by the hon. members on either side-especialf that of the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Boyce) that the local government of Ontario has a policy on this question reserving to themselves the exploitation of all water-powers, refusing to giye them to private companies.
I may interject here that I understood that the right hon. gentleman subscribed Mr. LENNOX.
to the doctrine that the policy of the local legislature having been enunciated, that policy would be respected on this occasion. The right hon. gentleman went on to say:
If we pass this Bill we interfere directly with this principle; and under those circumstances, holding as I have held all my life, to the sacredness, if the word is not too strong, of provincial rights, while we have the brute power to override those powers, it is a question whether we should do so, and it is a question upon which I would invite the serious consideration of my hon. friend who is promoting this Bill.
The right hon. gentleman_ has always on such occasions, not only to members on his own side of the House, but to members on this side, expressed himself in the politest possible language; and I understood him to give a very definite intimation to the hon. gentleman, though in polite language, that he had better drop the Bill. My impression was that from that time the Bill was dead, as I think it ought to be. But whether that was a correct construction of the right hon. gentleman's remarks or not, the Ontario government are justified in so understanding them, and if we are to act in such a way as to have harmony among the various units which constitute the Dominion of Canada, we must pay some regard to the wishes of the provinces or at least give them an opportunity to present their views to the House before we adopt legislation which is contrary to their express opinion. In that view, with the greatest respect, I urge upon the Prime Minister that whatever may be the ultimate outcome, it is not advisable to press this matter at this time. I am quite prepared to assume that the Prime Minister is just as anxious to promote harmony as myself- probably more so, because he occupies a more responsible position; but I think I can appeal to his judgment and to that of the committee, that it is not wise to press this matter forward without giving the local government an opportunity to present its views in a concise and considered form. In doing that, I think that time will not be lost, but rather gained, and the Prime Minister will be enunciating, even more distinctly than he did on the previous occasion, his adhesion to the principle of provincial rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend and I are very far apart, but he misapplies what I stated the other day. I said then, and I repeat to-day, that the only difficulty I see in this matter is on the question of expropriation. On that question I feel very strongly. When this matter was before the Private Bills Committee, I understand that the Ontario government was represented there, and that its representative informed the committee that the whole objection of that govern-

ment was to the expropriation clause. I do not understand that they questioned the jurisdiction of this parliament.
I have been informed by members of the provincial government that while they referred to the expropriation clause as an illustration, they had strong objection to our dealing with the matter at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The question of jurisdiction is a question on which we have pronounced already. The Minister of Justice is of opinion that we have jurisdic-' tion.
Does the Minister of Justice contend that the parliament of Canada has exclusive jurisdiction or concurrent jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know just what he said, as I have not his remarks at hand; but I have no hesitation for my part in saying that if we had concurrent jurisdiction, in all international matters the parliament of Canada should have paramount jurisdiction. The matter of jurisdiction we have settled, rightly or wrongly; we think rightly. Then the whole argument is on the question of expropriation.

My right hon. friend does me the compliment of saying that we are not very far apart, but I think we are, on one point. On the question of expropriation the right hon. gentleman took strong ground. That is one important feature of the matter; but there has been put forward by the Ontario government a feature which is even of greater importance, and which touches a more vital principle; that is, that the province has the right to legislate on this matter, and has a formulated policy upon it. It was upon that branch of the question that I undertook particularly to address myself to the right hon. gentleman, and to his statement, in effect, that as regards these water-powers the Ontario legislature has adopted a policy which this government is prepared to respect. The Ontario government says: We want to conserve the rights of the province for the people, and therefore we have adopted a certain policy as to water-powers by which we hope to create a great source of revenue for the people and incidentally develop great industries for the province. The right hon. gentleman the other day put it forward as the paramount consideration that we should respect the policy of the Ontario government on this matter; and on that point we have more reason to stay our hand to-day than we had on the 19th of April, because the Bill has been modified since that time, and it was only on Saturday that the modifications were placed before the Ontario government. The Ontario government intimate to my hon. friend from Peel that they want to have a say in this matter. Are we going to proceed in their absence not only to ignore their policy and to deprive the province of its rights, but to refuse even to grant them the courtesy of a hearing through their representative? I have every faith that my right hon. friend will see the expediency of allowing this matter to stand, and of allowing the government of Ontario to present their views before the House.
I wish to point out that the gentlemen who are asking for this legislation are chiefly from the United States-* Thomas Sturgis, of the city of New York, and J. C. Hunter, of the city of Duluth.
Read all the names. That is only two out of five.
The hon. gentleman is laying stress on the policy of the Ontario government, but he has not told the House what that policy is.
The hon. member for South Toronto explained it.

I think I know the policy of the Ontario government as well as most men, and there is no such policy as has been presented to this House. The Ontario government is giving charter after charter to companies to develop water-powers. When the representative of the Ontario government was before the Private Bills Committee at the time this Bill was under consideration, and was asked by one of the members if he claimed that there was the same right in the province as to a boundary water and a stream wholly within the province, his reply was that in the case of a boundary stream the rights of the province were not necessarily ousted, but there was a difference between the Nipigon river and the Pigeon river. When he was asked by myself if the land had long previously passed from the Crown, and if the riparian rights of the river were vested in a private owner, would the provincial policy be in the same position, he said that of couse that would make a difference, but he had no evidence that that was the case. Now, I think this committee has evidence that that is the case.
I have refrained all along from criticising or discussing the policy of the Ontario government; but if hon. gentlemen want to draw me into a discussion of the administration of the Ontario government, I do not shrink from the task.
Go on.

I am not going further just now in that direction. My hon. friend laboured to show that there was something in the statement made by the right hon. leader of the House which indicated that the Bill in its present form conflicted with the policy of the Ontario government. That is perhaps correct; I am not going to contravene it just now. The Tight hon. leader of the House was perfectly justified in taking the view he did; but what I ask is, even if that view be held with regard to the Nipigon river, there is no question Of pro-Mr. BLAIN.
vincial rights involved in the Nipigon river. /The Privy Council has held that section 92, now section 5, of the Navigable Water Protection Act, was within the jurisdiction of this parliament. Our courts have held that this parliament, and this parliament alone, has the right to deal with navigable waters. The leader of the House himself, when this Bill was at its second reading, held that the legislature had not the right to create a company to exercise the powers asked by this Bill, much less to give the power to deal with works proposed. Let me point out that this question is entirely in the hands of the government,, and that we on this side have confidence in the government. Section 18 provides that nothing can be done until the plans are approved of by the Governor in Council. What is the proceeding, supposing this Bill passes with powers of expropriation as to Pigeon river? Some lawyers tell me there are no powers of expropriation in this Bill, others tell me there are.
Subsection (d) of section 8 gives ample powers of expropriation.

I will take the hon. gentleman's word for it, I am glad to be able to agree with him for once. What I say is this, that under section 18 the procedure is defined. This company must get its plans approved of by the Board of Railway Commissioners, and before it does that it must get them ratified by the Governor in Council. It must sub-' mit a book of reference showing who the owners are, and whose rights are affected, without which no ratification will take place, either by the Governor in Council or by the Board of Railway Commissioners. If, at that stage of the proceeding, it is shown that the province of Ontario has interests that are being interfered with in any undue sense, it is entirely in the power of the government of the day to refuse to ratify the plans.
Is that the time to contest it? Rather would not this be the time to contest it?

No hon. gentleman on that side of the House has given one tittle of evidence, or quoted any judgment of the courts from which a conclusion can be drawn to support their contention; on the contrary, evidence that should not be disputed, evidence that is palpable, has been produced to show that there can be no possible contention that there are any provincial interests or provincial rights involved.

I will accept the hon. gentleman's challenge at once. But first I want to address myself to the Prime Minister in Tegard to this question of jurisdiction; I want to emphasize what I said on

Friday night about the difference between having jurisdiction and the wisdom of exercising it. The Minister of Justice says that we would have power-power to do a wrong, I daresay, in this matter. But the question of power rightly exercised and the question of jurisdiction, are entirely different things, they are entirely opposite, so far as regards the expediency of our dealing -with this matter. The Prime Minister says that if the objection as to expropriation were removed, where would be the reason for not dealing -with this Bill? The reason is that we are dealing with a Bill with which we have no business to deal. We are not the judges of what should be the policy of those who are rightly concerned in exercising that policy. We cannot say here what we would do if we were in the provincial legislature, we do not look at this matter with the same responsibility to the people, and therefore we do not have the same rights that the legislature would have. Now my hon. friend who is supporting this Bill just let the cat out of the bag by telling us that he differs from the policy of the provincial government in regard to these matters. That of itself ought to be a reason why we should not interfere with the policy of the provincial government.
I did not put it in that way; what I said was that the Ontario government had no such policy as the hon. gentleman represented, and that I had refused to criticise them on that ground.

The hon. gentleman is talking about a subsequent statement he made. Prior to the statement he has just repeated, he challenged us that if we wanted to discuss the propriety of the policy of the Ontario government in this matter he was prepared to show that it was not a good policy.
I did not say that.

Well, to that effect, that the policy of the Ontario government was not a good policy, which caused me to interrupt him and to say: Is that not why you are here? It must be manifest that the promoters of this Bill are here because they cannot get what they are asking for from the provincial government; that must he patent to everybody who is not a mere child. They would not be here after this legislation if they were satisfied to take what the Ontario government would give them, and I think that is confirmed by what the hon. gentleman has said. Now as to the exercise of this jurisdiction. It is contended apparently, not only by hon. gentlemen supporting this Bill, but I fancy by the Prime Minister, that if this is a navigable stream no power but the Dominion government has control of that stream
or any operations upon it for navigation. That Is true, I think; and here comes an answer to the challence of the hon. gentleman that we could quote no authority to show that the province had any rights in a stream that was navigable. Let me give the hon. gentleman a couple of authorities that he can find in Cartwright's Cases on the British North America Act. Let him go to the library and look up volume 2, page 542, in the case of MacMillan versus Southwest Boom Company, where the decision is in these words:
Subsection 10, of section 91, of the British North America Act gives the right merely to prescribe rules and regulations for vessels navigating the waters of the Dominion, and not as excluding for all purposes provincial jurisdiction over navigable waters.

Does the hon. gentleman seriously wish to assert that I have set up any contention of that kind? My argument was that the Ontario legislature has not the power to deal with the question embodied in this Bill.
Now, the question embodied in this Bill, so far as jurisdiction goes, is whether the Ontario government has power to deal with this stream, it being admitted to be a navigable stream.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not the point.

I think that is the point. If it is a navigable stream, this government has supreme jurisdiction in reference to navigation. But this case I have just quoted shows that section 91 of the British North America Act does not transfer a river to the Dominion jurisdiction merely because it is navigable, but only gives the right to prescribe rules and regulations for vessels navigating the waters of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In my judgment the paramount consideration in this matter is not whether the Pigeon river is navigable-I do not know whether it is or not-but the paramount consideration is that it is an international stream.

Before coming to that, I will give another authority to my hon. friend so that he may see there is evidence, and that he need not challenge anybody hereafter to produce it. In the case of the Central Vermont Railway vs. St. Johns, 4 Cartwright, page 331, it is held:
The control over navigation conferred on the Dominion parliament by the British North America Act does not prevent the provincial legislature from exercising municipal and police control on navigable waters.
The principle is the same; there is a certain amount of control and interest vested in the province in regard to any stream

within the province, that is not required to be exercised in regard to the protection of it for navigation purposes. Let us be clear on this point. My hon. friend, or the promoters of this Bill, are not asking for anything that interferes with navigation, that is to say, in regard to the jurisdiction that this government possesses. He is not chartering a line of ships, or wanting to build wharfs or anything else affecting navigation and trade and commerce, things which are meant to be covered by the British North America Act. But he is giving a commercial company power to produce goods, to sell, to produce commodities, to make profits out of them, which he has a right to do, a commendable right to do, or his promoters have, if they go to the proper place for the power. Now it is not necessary for any one to have a Dominion charter to manufacture anything in this country and sell it in another country; it is no more necessary for him to have a Dominion charter to manufacture and sell one thing in this country than another.
The Canadian Niagara Power Company is doing business on the Niagara river today under provincial jurisdiction alone. It came to this parliament and asked for a charter but it finally withdrew the application when it found Dominion government legislation was not necessary. It did not want rights that the Ontario government would not give it and it is carrying on practically the same business as my hon. friend's incorporators want to carry on under the powers of this parliament. It is, I fancy, the largest concern there is in this line of business. It is operating solely under provincial charter, upon a navigable river and iipon an international boundary -not navigable at the point where it is operating, but certainly international, and when the right hon. prime minister raises the point as to this river being navigable and international, both are covered by the case of the Niagara river. No one can say that the Niagara river is not an international boundary. This company is to-day doing the very kind of business on a very large scale under a provincial charter that the hon. gentleman's incorporators ask us to permit them to do by a Dominion charter. There is no necessity of this charter for the purpose of tloing anything over which the Dominion has control, that is over navigation. I repeat that if this charter were being asked for in regard to marine matters, in regard to vessels, shipping or wharfs, or anything having to do with navigation, there might be some reason for saying that we should grant it. But this matter has nothing to do with navigation and therefore our powers in regard to navigation cannot be exercised. Even as the Prime Minister says, if this is an international stream, all they ask to do can be done under a provincial charter. They can manufacture their goods and export them Mr. LANCASTER.
the same as the Canadian Niagara Power Company is doing to-day. They are subject to no Dominion law but one and that is in regard to the exportation of power. They can manufacture it under a provincial charter just the same as any other man can manufacture clothing, or axes, or anything else that he has a charter from the provincial government to manufacture and he does not need to come to the Dominion. There seems to me to be no possible ground left for argument that there is any need to come to this parliament for a charter at all and, holding that view, I think that we ought not to pass even what we think is a harmless part of this Bill. I cannot see how we make it any better by passing clauses which we think do not do much harm. We are not the judges as to whether they do or do not. It is a question for the province as a matter of policy and of knowledge because they must be the best judges of their own affairs. In dealing with provincial assets, with provincial rights, with revenue from royalties and from other assets, the right of manufacturing electricity from water-power, which is certainly a valuable privilege each province has the right to decide those questions for itself and when we are asked to deal with them at all we ought to refuse to do so and not pass such a Bill as this on the simple asertion that it would appear that the clause is harmless.	.

The hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Con-mee) seems to be of the opinion that the proprietary interest in the Canadian side of the Pigeon river lies within the jurisdiction of the province. I would like to know if that is his opinion.
My answer to that would be that it belongs at present to the riparian owners of the land along the shore and that the government parted with any interest they ever had in 1856.

If the contention of the hon. gentleman is right then these riparian owners could prevent navigation and shipping. If the proprietary interest in the waters belongs to the riparian owners they might 'prevent navigation and shipping in any form.

I would answer that question by saying ' no,' that the riparian owners have, not control over the waters. I am advised that there is no such thing as ownership in waters. The Privy Council, in a decision which has been read in this debate, decided that the parliament of Canada alone has the legislative jurisdiction over not only boundary streams but over navigable streams. I will read a sentence here from a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada on that point. This was the case of the Queddy River Driving and

Boom Company vs. Davidson, 1883, 3 Cartwright, page 243. Mr. Justice Strong in that case, at page 257 of the law reports, used this language:
No one can deny that by subsection 10 of section 91 of the British North America Act, exclusive power to legislate respecting navigation is conferred on the parliament of Canada, and as little is it open to any one to dispute that this power respecting navigation includes the exclusive right to legislate so as to authorize an obstruction in a navigable public river.

I thought that the hon. gentleman had come to a wrong conclusion. The hon. gentleman has apparently come to the conclusion, that, because the British North America Act gave the Dominion parliament certain power with respect to navigation and shipping, therefore it gave them a proprietary interest in the waters of the river. The reverse is held to be the case. The law, as I understand it, is that unless you can show a proprietary interest in rivers and waters which have been transferred from the ownership of the provincial legislature to that of the Dominion legislature by virtue of the British North America Act, the proprietary rights which the province formerly enjoyed still remain vested in the province, and that the only right that the Dominion government can assume is in respect of navigation and shipping. It has been held in many cases that under the words ' navigation and shipping ' the Dominion does not acquire a proprietary interest in waters but has simply the right to regulate navigation and shipping in those waters. I would point to the case referred to by my hon. friend from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster) of the Vermont Central Railway vs. the town of St. Johns. In that case the town of St. Johns had passed a by-law extending its corporation limits to the centre of the Richelieu river. Across the Richelieu river there had been erected a bridge and the town claimed the right to assess one half of the bridge because they say it lay within the corporation of St. Johns. They did assess it and the company appealed against the assessment on the ground that it was a navigable river and also upon the ground that the corporation had no right to make that assessment. But the court upheld the contention of the town and held that the town was the owner of the river bed to the centre of the river. The Chief Justice in that case summed up as follows, and I would like my hon. friend to follow this:
Navigation and shipping are words used by the British North America Act. That does not mean the river at all. The river itself belongs to the local Crown domain.
That seems to put it quite clearly, that the river itself belongs to the local Crown
domain. How do we apply that to the present case? That means that one half of the bed of the river belongs to the local Crown domain, the local Crown domain is the province of Ontario, and once you give this company proprietary ot expropriation rights you are interfering with the rights of the province in one half of that river.
If my hon. friend is right in saying that was granted by the Crown in 1856, how could it belong to the province in 1856?

According to this decision the river itself belongs to the local Crown domain and my hon. friend says a private person can have no proprietary rights in water. That is quite true. Therefore, if private parties can have no proprietary rights in water it still remains that the river itself belongs to the local Crown domain under the decision I have referred to.
Cannot the Crown grant it?
But even if the right is granted against the province you could not take half of this river.
But if the Crown granted it.
My hon. friend said the Crown had no right to grant what the individual had no right to own, a proprietary interest in a river.
Does the hon. member attribute that language to me?
I have to accept my hon. friend's explanation but I understood him to say that.
I never even thought oE such an argument as that.
I recollect quite distinctly that the other day the hon gentleman argued that because the river was a navigable river, authority over it was exclusively within the Dominion jurisdiction.
I argued that.

Now he says that the river at the point where he wishes to exercise proprietary rights, is bounded on each side by rocky cliffs and therefore cannot be navigable. I thus fail to see how he can give this parliament jurisdiction because it is a navigable river.

The parliament of Canada in 1856 and 1857 laid out a canal and the levels, profiles, plans and everything in connection with building locks right along this very river are of record in the department here, so it is a navigable river in every sense.
Does the hon. gentleman raise any claim to jurisdiction of this parliament because of the Pigeon river being a navigable river?

My contention all along has been that this parliament, and _ this parliament alone, has legislative jurisdiction over boundary rivers, and in my judgment over navigable rivers. That has been my argument and I do not recede from it at all.

I do not think my hon. friend's contention is in line with the contention of the first minister, who a few minutes ago said he did not place any reliance upon this parliament having jurisdiction because it was a navigable river, he based his contention on its being an international river. With respect to the Pigeon river being an international river I fail to see yet, subject to conversion hereafter, why the mere fact that the Pigeon riveT is an international river gives this parliament exclusive jurisdiction. I would ask the hon. gentleman opposite if the province of Ontario could not give the promoter of this Bill just as great rights to build his plant to the boundary line between this country and the United States as this parliament can?
No.
It has been done in other cases?
No.

Under tne legislation of the province of Ontario my hon. friend could build his lines right to the boundary line, but if he wanted to go one inch further he would have to go to the government [DOT]f a foreign country to obtain greater powers, just as if legislation was passed by this parliament, and he would then later come before this parliament. In order to give this parliament jurisdiction we have to insert the words 'for the general advantage of Canada,' and if that clause had been retained this parliament would have had jurisdiction; but I am glad to say that the Minister of Justice has seen fit to declare that the work is not for the general benefit of Canada, and not being for the general benefit of Canada we have the right to assume that the company is local in its undertaking. I do not think any hon. gentleman can undertake to say it is not local, and for this reason it cannot gain by authority of this parliament what the province of Ontario can not give it. I grant further that if the company were seeking power to carry lines from one province into another this parliament would have jurisdiction, because- we have the right of jurisdiction to legislate and give Mr. CONMEE.
power to a company to build lines into an adjoining province, but not to go beyond the international boundary. This company is confined exclusively to the province of Ontario, and its works not being declared for the general advantage of Canada why not relegate it entirely to the province of Ontario, to which they beong?
Leaving the question of jurisdiction, we have in Ontario a hydro-electric commission inaugurated for the very purpose of developing such natural resources as are proposed to be given to this company, and can any hon. gentleman say that the province of Ontario will not administer these assets more in the interests of Ontario than would the promoters and members of this company. I take the broad ground that it is beyond doubt more advantageous to the people of Ontario to have the hydroelectric commission administer these water-powers. I fail to see why we should interfere in this matter at all. When the Bill first came up owing to the strenuous objections of members on this side of the House some of the objectionable features were removed, but I contend that we should now leave the matter entirely in the hands of the local legislature and let them deal with it in accordance with their policy.

I have a good deal of sympathy for the promoter of this Bill in his effort to hold up his end against legal men on this side. I would ask the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if the Canadian section of the International Waterways Commission have been asked to pass upon this measure?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not aware that they have.
The Bill provides that before anything is done the plans must be ratified by the Waterways Commission.

We have the Waterways Commission which was called into existence by an Act of the Congress of the United States of June 13, 1902, which calls upon Canada to join in the appointment of a joint commissioner to deal with the waters which discharge into the Atlantic ocean by the St. Lawrence river. The waters dealt with in this Bill are covered by that Act of Congress. That commission has reported to the government from time to time as to the method of dealing with international waters. I find in a report addressed to the Minister of Public Works in 1906 this statement:
Diversions of international waters elsewhere than at Niagara river or the Niagara peninsula should only be permitted;
(a)	For domestic purposes and for the service of locks in navigation canals:
(b)	Temporary diversions, where the water taken is returned again, only on the recommendation of the joint commission.

Now that commission likewise in a report to the Minister of Public Works in March, 1908, used this language when dealing with the Niagara Falls situation:
While we think it should be a condition of the charters of all companies hereafter incorporated in Canada that the power generated should be distributed wholly in this country-
There is no misunderstanding that language. We are endeavouring in this Bill to dispose of some waters that belong to somebody. Some gentlemen claim that they belong to the province of Ontario; others claim that they should be dealt with by this House. Assuming that they should be dealt with by this government, I would like to know if there is any department of our government engaged in their administration. They are the most valuable asset we possess. They will last as long as the country lasts; they will furnish us with our power, light and heat in the future. These water-powers must have some value. To some minds they have a very great value; but it appears to me that the parliament of Canada, not only at present, but in the past, has been disposing too freely of the valuable assets of this country. As long as I have a seat in this House I am going to oppose that in every possible way. The waters of this country belong to the people of this country, and they should be conserved for the benefit of the people; and the waters which are within the boundaries of the province of Ontario should be handled by that province. For these reasons I am determinedly opposed to any Bill of this kind. The purpose of this company is to export this power. The government has an opinion from one of their own officials that that should not be done, and in view of that fact, why should the time of parliament be taken up in discussing this matter? The utmost ignorance exists with regard to the extent of this wateT-power, and I am decidedly opposed to it being handed over to a private company.
At one o'clock committee adjourned.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

We all agree in the Prime Minister's statement that a great deal of time has been taken up with the discussion of this Bill and that it should be disposed of as soon as possible, but the loss of time is the fault not of the committee but of the promoter of the Bill. The Prime Minister contended that because the Pigeon river is an international stream, its waters flowing between Canada and the state of Minnesota, this parliament is, ipso facto, given jurisdiction over it. I do not accede to that statement as there is no authority for such a proposition in either the British North America Act or any judicial decision
of which I am awaTe. I take the view that if these are provincial wateTs, as I believe they are, the Dominion has no greater rights of an international nature than the provinces would have, that is that the British authority on this side of the line cannot invade the territorial waters or the jurisdiction of the state of Minnesota, and that the Crown in Tight of the province of On; tario is the proper tribunal to deal with these questions, if it is necessary to have dealings with the United States. The Canadian right in that respect is vested in the province just as it was before confederation, and by virtue of section 109 of the British North America Act the province is continued in its ownership of the land over which the water flows. It seems folly to say that this parliament has the right to grant the powers asked for by this Bill when it is evident upon the face of the legislation that the regulation of all such matters, the regulation of municipal and police matters and the enforcement of law, all fall within the provincial domain. I ask the right hon. gentleman to consider this matter in the same way. I again call his attention to the conditon on the Niagara river where we have the pioneer company, the Canadian Niagara Power Company, originally getting a charter in 1892 from the province of Ontario and operating under that charter ever since.
I am informed on very good authority that that company has come here and obtained a charter since then.
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken.
The evidence will show it has done that.

There is no such legislation to be found in the statutes of Canada. The Canadian Electrical Development Company and the Ontario Company, which are the only other two companies operating on the Niagara river, went first to the Ontario government and made a bargain with that province before coming here and that is what we ask these promoters to do, to make their bargain with the province of Ontario and then come here as the other companies came to have their bargains ratified and incorporated in our statutes, then if any difference arises between the parties to the bargain, the province of Ontario and the company, the matter can come before a more or less independent tribunal, the parliament of Canada. The elimination of the Nipigon river modifies the intensity of the opposition to this Bill but in its relation to the Pigeon river it is still objectionable.

The hon. gentleman says that all other companies have acquired agreements from the province of Ontario before coming here. I have here the Act of

the Ontario and Erie Power Company, a company incorporated here, and there is not one word in that Act with regard to any agreement with the province.
That company is not in operation at all.
But its charter was granted.
It is not operating and never has operated.

And that charter has
been renewed twice. The hon. gentleman allowed it to be renewed this year and did not say a word against it.
It does not contain the same clause as this.

The same clause exactly from the Railway Act and it gives a great deal wider powers. It gives the company power to take the waters of the Welland river and the Jordan river and to divert them through to Lake Ontario, to widen these rivers and take them out of their regular course. It also gives the company power to take the waters of Lake Erie and to divert them into Lake Ontario. There is no comparison between the scope of their Act and the one now before the House.

The Erie Bill passed this House some years ago but the company has never gone into operation. They propose to take water from a system of waters known as the Welland canal. The Welland river is part of the Welland canal waterway, which, as we all know, is a work not only within the jurisdiction of this parliament but constructed by this parliament and they had to come here to obtain power to use the waters of the Welland canal.
What about Lake Erie and the Jordan river?
The Jordan river is practically part of the Welland canal system too.
The canal is not only a Dominion work but a Dominion-owned work.

Admitting for the sake of argument-and of course we do not admit it-that this parliament has exclusive jurisdiction to deal with this question and that the provinces have no jurisdiction whatever, should not this government have some policy in regard to this and similar assets? We ought to have a declaration of policy from the govenment. Is it their policy to alienate to private companies these important assets, suppose they do belong to the Dominion? I have heard a great deal about the policy of the Ontario Mr. CONMEE.
government in an opposite direction, and we ought to have some declaration with regard to the policy of this government. Is, it their policy to alienate in perpetuity valuable public assets to private companies?

At this late stage of the session, when we are anxious to bring our work to a close, it is very unfortunate that this Bill should be brought up again. When the right hon. gentleman turned it down the otheT day, we thought we had heard the last of it for this session at least, but we have it popping up again like an irrepressible jack-in-the-box. The legal aspect of the question has been fully discussed, and I do not think it can be seriously pretended that this government has exclusive jurisdiction. Even if the British North America Act be strained to give it some jurisdiction, at least the Ontario government have rights in these water-powers within their own province, and ought to be left free to deal with them. We are told that the Bill passed the committee, but we must remember that it passed at a rather stormy meeting and contrary to the vote of the Ontario members, both Liberal and Conservative. It only passed by virtue of the vote of members from the other provinces who are not directly interested and who were drummed up for that purpose. I know that Ontario members on the Liberal side remained away and refused to vote for the Bill but did not like to appear and vote against it out of regard for my hon. friend the promoter of "the Bill (Mr. Conmee). I hope that no one imagines that we on this side oppose the measure because my hon. friend is the promoter. We would oppose it just as strongly if it were put forward by an hon. member on this side. We are opposing it on principle, because we believe it is of vital importance to the province of Ontario that that province should have control in this matter, and if necessary we are prepared to oppose it from day to day and thus prolong this session which we all desire to see brought to an end. I think the right hon. the Prime Minister has been ill advised in giving his consent to have this Bill brought up again. We must remember that the company in question is largely controlled by American citizens, who will no doubt, in the working out of the measure place the interest of their own country first. Let me remind the House that when the Niagara Power Company Bill was brought in a year ago, we took the precaution to provide that only the surplus power should be sold on the other side of the line, but no such precaution is taken in this measure, and the company may sell the greater part of its power in the United States. Under the circumstances, the Bill is a most dangerous one. The Ontario government have appointed an electric commis-

sion which has done good work in the province of Ontario, and that policy has been endorsed by an overwhelming majority of the free and independent electors of that province. If there is one Act more than another of the Ontario government which the people appreciate it is their reserving of these powers for the province. Under the circumstances, it would be a blunder and a crime against the province of Ontario if we should pass this Bill. This House ought not to put itself in a hostile attitude to any province. We ought to remember that our water-powers are the greatest assets which our provinces possess. They are the white coal of the country, to which we look to take the place of the ordinary coal when that is exhausted. Under the circumstances we ought to be very careful not to give a perpetual franchise which will take this power out of the province altogether. This is one of the greatest water-powers we have in that part of the country. Without going into the legal question, it seems to me that the province is better fitted to deal with this asset than is the Dominion parliament.
