Charters of this kind are usually given by the Ontario government; and if this session be delayed on account of this Bill, the responsibility must Test on this government.

My hon. friend who is promoting the Bill made two propositions a moment ago, and I think only two mistakes. One of his statements was that the Canadian Niagara Power Company, although refused a charter in the first instance, had come to this parliament again and obtained one. If that is the case it would have been very easy for the hon. gentleman to have proved his statement. But let me point out that when that company applied for a charter the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) opposed its application, and after having pointed out that he had done so at the instance of a number of influential Liberals and others in his own riding and elsewhere in the province of Ontario, he succeeded in getting a few weeks adjournment, and the Bill never came forward again. The company withdrew its application and so the matter ended as it should have done. That was one of the hon. gentleman's propositions during his last speech. But it did not apply prejudicially to the company, a company carrying on business effectively and successfully, and the largest business of any of the development companies that exist on the Niagara river, and so far as I know, they are experiencing no difficulty. The hon. gentleman also referred to the Ontario Power Company. I think he should have left the Ontario Power Company alone, because we have before us the report of the commission appointed by this government to look after our water-powers 170

and international streams. The commission is composed of Mr. Geo. C. Gibbins, Mr. Louis Coste, and Mr. Wm. J. Stewart. We have their supplemental report; and I would think that the members who support the government and the government would be prepared to abide in the main by the recommendations of their commission. They deal with this Ontario Power Company, and they point out how unfortunate it is that these three companies were incorporated and given such large powers before public attention had been directed to the importance of keeping these great sources of wealth in the control of the provinces. It is important that the government should pay some heed to the statements contained in this report, and I will take the liberty of referring to a few of them. Later on, if the government does not see fit to adhere to the proposition of the Prime Minister on the 19th of April last, and if he is disposed to recede from the position taken that evening, I shall have occasion to refer more at length to the contents of this report. In the meantime they say:
It is manifest that some arrangement must be arrived at between the two countries with regard to the regulation and use of the boundary waters, otherwise chaos will prevail. At Niagara, on each side of the river, charters had been granted under which water in unlimited quantities could have been taken at points further up the river. On our side it was sought to use the Chippewa river to drain the waters of Niagara into a new outlet-a canal to be built to a point near St. David's. Another Canadian charter sought to divert the waters of Lake Erie to a point near Jordan.
That is the Ontario Power Company.
On the New York side there was no limitation to the water which could be taken under several charters.
Now here is what these gentlemen say with reference to this matter:
All these proposed developments would affect, more or less seriously, the level of Lake Erie, and all are objectionable on that account, and wholly opposed to the principle adopted by the commission.
What is the government going to do about it? Are they going to let the recommendations of this committee go for nothing, ot are they going to abide by their recommendations? The committee say further:
The diversion of 10,000 cubic feet per second would have a more serious effect upon the level of Lake Erie than the diversion from Lake Michigan, at Chicago, of a like amount. It would mean the reduction of the lake level by more than six inches.

So we are not here to justify the Ontario Power Company, we are here to show that before the attention of the people had been called to this question, three power companies had been incorporated in reference to the Niagara river, and it is a most unfortunate thing that these three power companies were incorporated at that time. But as they are incorporated, it is for the government to see to it that no further companies are incorporated with a like result. In reference to another proposition that the hon. gentleman and some other hon. gentlemen, have repeated, let me show what this commission says, after speaking of international waters:
Neither company has any right of property, but only a right of user, in these flowing waters.
Further on they say:
It, perhaps, would have been wise if development had been limited to the generation of electricity for distribution in Canada.
That is the position I took the other evening, that is the position I take now, and that I intend to maintain, namely: That it is not in the interest of Canada or the Canadian people that we should transmit power to the United States to help build up American industries at the expense of our own development. If, by a proper protective tariff, as has been shown, and I called the right hon. gentleman's attention to it the other day, 134 large firms in the United States have been compelled to plant large industries in Canada, if that is in the interest of Canada, and undoubtedly it is, is it not in the interest of Canada, where we have this God-given power in the great rivers and water falls we possess, that we should keep that power within our own hands, and compel people who want to benefit by the natural resources of Canada to come into our territory, and build up our markets and our country by establishing industries within our own limits? Now they say it would have been wise if development had been limited to the generation of electricity for distribution in Canada, and add:
In that case w© would most likely have had only one corporation up to this time, and, moreover, would have had the Canadian market fully supplied.
Now I particularly desire to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to this position taken by this commission. At page 15 they say:
The control over one-half of the production would undoubtedly supply all the demands of our Canadian market for many years to come, and it would not be any great hardship ^upon the companies to compel them to jointly or severally build the necessary transmission lines to care for the same.

The commission is here dealing with the three companies that had already been incorporated, and they are pointing out that although certain rights have been conceded to these companies, it is inadvisable that they should be allowed to other companies making application, or to this company now making application, the first since this report has been brought in. The commission had knowledge of the fact that my hon. friend had a Bill of this class, and they point out that it is not advisable to have any further companies incorporated in Canada. They say:
While we think it should be a condition of the charters of all companies hereafter incorporated in Canada that the power generated should be distributed wholly in this country, that principle cannot with fairness be applied to these corporations at Niagara Falls.
So the whole result of the argument of the commission is that we cannot apply the proper principle to the three companies who have already acquired vested rights in regard to the export of power, but that to all future companies we should apply the principle that no export shall be permitted to the United States.
It would be monstrous if all but 40,000 or 50,000 horse-power of the total 400,000 development should find a market in New York State. The public in western Ontario are thoroughly aroused against this threatened injustice.
I do not so much appeal to the right hon. first minister because naturally-and I do not say this offensively-I cannot get his ear to the same extent as can his loyal and faithful supporters. But, whilst I urge upon him most respectfully to take a broader view of this question I also protest against our acting in such a way as shall prevent any province from developing, for the benefit of its own people, the natural resources of that province.

I would like to press my question upon the first minister. Admitting, for the sake of argument, the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion, admitting, that the province has no power at all, is it wisdom on our part to alienate these water-powers to a company in perpetuity without providing for some compensation, or for the right to collect royalty, or without regulation of any kind except as provided in this Bill? What is the policy that should actuate us in dealing with these water-powers and other natural resources and in disposing of them to private companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have expressed more than once what the views of the government are on this matter and I am sorry if I have failed to make myself understood. As to the question of jurisdiction we claim that it is vested in this par-

liament. I have said again and again that 1 thought we had the power to deal with this Bill. The question which is in the mind of my hon. friend (Mr. S. Sharpe) is the question of the right of expropriation. Shall we allow this company to expropriate these water-powers or not? That is a matter which would not logically come up under this clause. I have stated to the promoter of the Bill that on this point I have an open mind and that I would not decide the matter one way or the other. Until we reach this point I do not think it is proper for me to offer any advice. I keep a perfectly open mind. The government have not formulated a policy upon this matter because we have had very little opportunity of dealing with such questions. It is admitted that in dealing with the Nipigon river, though a navigable stream, we should defer to the provincial government, but with regard to an international stream we certainly have the control in our own hands. Whether or not w'e should allow this company to take the power of expropriation is a matter as to which we should reserve our views until we come to the discussion of the question.

Mr. Chairman, the Bill before the committee has been discussed at very great length and I have no doubt that all that can be said on the subject has been said. The argument that- is of compelling force, to my mind, has, however, not been put as expressly as I would hope to put it. If I can succeed in presenting it I shall be very brief and I trust that I shall have the ear of those who are closely concerned with this measure. I fancy the Tight hon. first minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) misapprehends, in to a very great degree, the basis upon which the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) founds his claim to exclusive jurisdiction in this parliament. The Minister of Justice founded his claim upon an asseveration that this Bill embodies in its form an assertion of power to export the product that the company pronoses to manufacture; that is to say, that by virtue of the power embodied in the Bill to export power to other provinces and across the line, by virtue of that clause and that clause alone, this parliament has jurisdiction. If the first minister will look at the speech of the Minister of Justice he will find that it was on that ground that the Minister of Justice based his assertion and his conclusions that this parliament alone had jurisdiction. The Minister of Justice, in pressing that claim, admitted that if this company, promoted by the hon. member for Bainv River (Mr. Conmee), had gone to the provincial government of Ontario and had obtained a charter, leaving out 'entirely the clause which asks for power to export to other countries and other provinces, the company would, having obtained its 170*
charter, have, by virtue of what is called in the legal profession, the comity of nations, power to export to other provinces and other countries just the same as if the clause had been included. The position of the Minister of Justice then is that the inclusion of this clause in the Bill confers on us exclusive jurisdiction, but that if the clause were out and the Bill then went to the legislature of Ontario, which, in that event, would have the exclusive jurisdiction (because there is no such thing as concurrent jurisdiction), then the company would have the power which my hon. friend claims for it. Well, if that is so, if the argument of the Minister of Justice is right, the only reason for the inclusion in the Bill of this particular clause asking for power to export to other provinces and other countries is to confer upon this House exclusive jurisdiction. It is admitted that if that were not there those powers could be granted, aside entirely from what I might call the obiter dicta of the Minister of Justice in his remarks, by the Ontario legislature and they alone and the company would have all the powers they desired and could exercise them just the same as if this Bill had passed this House.
Now, the Minister of Justice, in opening his remarks, about two weeks ago, stated that in his opinion this work was not for the general advantage of Canada, and he said that in his opinion it was unwise and not right for this parliament to insert what was on its face incorrect, and consequently that he had advised the hon. member for Rainy River to leave that out. He deprecated the principle of importing into a Bill a fiction for the purpose of giving this parliament jurisdiction. I accept that principle in its entirety and I think all the members of this House will accept it as far as it goes. But, press it a litle farther and what is the effect of it? The hon. member for Rainy River brings exclusive jurisdiction into this parliament by includng in this Bill a clause asking for power to export to other countries and other provinces. Is not that a fiction? The Minister of Justice told us that we had no right, now that the Bill had passed the committee, to question the bona tides of the promoters of the Bill, to question the bona fides of their intention to export power to other countries and other provinces. I do not question their bona fides, but no matter what company comes here and asks for power it can, with equal bona fides, place in its Bill an application for power to export to other provinces and other countries. That can be put in with equal bona fides by all companies. Therefore, I say it amounts purely to a fiction. There is no necessity of giving any opinion whatever upon the admission of the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice and

the government are quite willing to lay down the principle that it is not right, that it is bad policy for this House to import one fiction into a Bill for the purpose of giving it jurisdiction, but that it is all right to import another. I, as one member of this House, would wish to exercise no jurisdiction that is based upon such a flimsy excuse as that. It would simply amount to this: that we, by virtue of a clause which any company in the world would be justified, in all good faith, in inserting in its Bill, could, in every case, assert to ourselves exclusive jurisdiction and make that, not a reason because it would not be a reason, but simply an excuse for passing such Bill in this House.

How does the hon. member deal with the fact of the development being upon an international stream and that the works must extend from side to side of the river so that the water must be affected on the American as well as on the Canadian side.

I quite appreciate the point raised by my hon. friend, and I appreciate also his anxiety to get away from the point I am now discussing. The Minister of Justice did mention that, but at present I am simply arguing that the basis laid down by the Minister of Justice as bringing into this House the exclusive jurisdiction was not a basis on which it was within the domain of this House to act.
Where do you find that in 'Hansard ?'

The hon. gentleman has experience in questioning members on this side of the House as to what appears in 'Hansard' but he seems not to have profited by the experience. On page 4592 'Hansard,' April 19, the Minister of Justice stated:
I have not made my meaning clear to my hon. friend if he thinks my remarks do not apply to the Nipigon river. This Bill proposes, as I have pointed out, to incorporate a company to manufacture electric energy by water-power on the Pigeon river and on the Nipigon river, and the electric energy so manufactured, no matter whether on' the Nipigon or on the Pigeon, this Bill proposes that the company shall have the power to transmit and sell for use at any place in the united States. There is no distinction, on the face of the Bill, between the power to be manufactured by the water of Pigeon river and that which is to be manufactured by the water of the Nipigon river. I speak without knowledge but my supposition is that the company do not intend to distinguish at all, m their operation, between the power manufactured at the one place and that manufactured at the other. The Nipigon is some 60 miles to the eastward of the cities of Port Arthur and Fort William, the Pigeon river is some 40 or 50 miles on the other side.

To abbreviate, the Minister of Justice goes on to argue that there is no distinction between one river and the other; basing his argument on the fact that the power to export is included, and, at page 4593 'Hansard,' in answer to a question by the member for West Algoma, the Minister of Justice said:
The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) asks me if in my opinion the fact that this Bill empowers the company to sell its products beyond the boundaries of the province gives this parliament exclusive jurisdiction over it. If I am to answer that question exactly as it is put, I would say yes. At the same time it is a legal question by no means free from doubt and one which has been recently under consideration.
He goes on to argue that it will likely not be until it comes before the Privy Council in England that that question will be finally decided, although he gave his opinion without qualification to this House. It is true, as the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) has said and is just about to say again, that on the same page of 'Hansard' the Minister of Justice does state that because the Pigeon river is an international stream this House has exclusive jurisdiction.

Does my hon. friend not see-without using any offensive language- that his argument is unfair. He is picking out from the remarks of the Minister of Justice a reply to a question put by the member for West Algoma with regard to the export of power. That is only incidental to the argument of the Minister of Justice and not a part of it.

It is the whole basis of his argument, and that is why the question was put by the member for West Algoma. In the body of his argument the Minister of Justice did state that the fact that the Pigeon river was an international stream gave exclusive jurisdiction to this parliament, but the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) will also see that in the body of that argument the Minister of Justice goes into no details. He gives nothing on which he bases that conclusion whereas in the other case he built up the entire construction of the speech he made to this House and goes into the most explicit details. But, supposing that we were to grant that this is an international stream and that consequently for certain purposes exclusive jurisdiction is in this parliament, will the Minister of Justice, or will any lawyer on the other side of the House deny that the province of Ontario would have power to incorporate a company that would build a dam, at least to the international boundary in the middle of the stream. Certainly, Ontario would have that power. Has this parliament of Canada any further power? Has this parliament of Canada any power to incorporate a company to build past the middle of

the stream? Surely not. Surely there is jurisdiction in the province of Ontario in so far as the purposes of a purely local and commercial undertaking are concerned to go just as far as the Dominion of Canada in that respect. Now then, to get to the kernel of the contention of the hon. gentleman-if there is any kernel to his contention-if after this company has obtained from the province of Ontario power to build to the middle of the stream; after they have obtained from the adjoining states to the south power to build to the same point from the American boundary, then, if any power to connect so as to utilize the two together be necessary to come from this House, which I very much doubt, then doubtless this company can come to this House and get that power. In that way we will grant all the power that it is necessary for us to grant and we will not interfere with the policy of the Ontario or any other province. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) only wants to come to this House for power to connect, and that is all he can come to this House for without interfering with provincial rights; if he wants to come to this House for such legislation then probably he would succeed because the principle of provincial rights would be in no way impaired thereby. The company he wishes power for would get at least all the power that the province of Ontario under their well endorsed policy could give them and that is all this company has any right to have or that this parliament has any right to give them. I have said as much as I intend to say on that point. I have not perhaps gone into this question quite as fully as my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) but sometimes by simply listening to his argument and by simply watching the very many beautiful manceuverings of my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) one can come to a conclusion perhaps more quickly and just as sound as he could by going into the authorities for himself.

I have listened to this argument and have read pretty carefully the debate which took place on the 19th of April, and I am forced to the conclusion that this seems to be a dispute between the supporters of the Ontario government on the one side and the hon. member for Rainy River on the other. But there are other members in this House who are_compelled to vote upon this question and we are therefore justified in giving our reasons for our belief. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) has not done himself justice this afternoon, and I want to say that he is usually very fair and very logical in his arguments. He cited from the speech of the Minister of Justice, but he only cited from that speech the remarks in reference to the exportation of electricity. I do not think that was fair, because had he gone to the
bottom of the same page he would have found the reason upon which the Minister of Justice had based his conclusion and which was this same subsection 10 of section 92 of the British North America Act, which contains certain exceptions as to the authority of the local legislatures, one of which exceptions is:
Local works and undertakings, other than such as are of the following classes:-
(a) Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
The Minister of Justice went on to explain this point, and in his judgment it came within the exceptions of subsection 10 of section 92, because it was a work extending beyond the limits of the province of Ontario, and therefore the jurisdiction 'could only be in this parliament. I will read his words:	,
At all events that is the proposition on the face of the Bill, and the observations I have made apply as much to the water-power at Nipigon as to that on the Pigeon river. I cannot understand how water-power could be utilized on the Pigeon river otherwise than by the construction of a dam across that river, which would have one end necessarily on American soil, and this parliament alone would have the power to incorporate a company for that purpose.
Had my hon. friend quoted that portion-
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I stated clearly that the minister had made that statement.

Well, I will leave the House to judge whether the hon. member read that as he started to do, or whether after he was challenged he made a statement somewhat along those lines. However, that is a small matter, the question is to get at the facts. We are told that the Pigeon river is about 300 feet across, and that there is a water-fall at that point; so that in order to develop power it would be necessary to erect a dam across the river. I cannot make the argument any stronger than the Minister of Justice made it. In view of the fact that to develop a waterpower it would be necessary to build a dam across the river, it is certain that the legislature of Ontario has no jurisdiction and that this parliament alone has jurisdiction. I am content to take the ground taken by the right hon. first minister, that when we are dealing with international rivers, this parliament should have jurisdiction and it should not be relegated to any provincial legislature. I believe the underlying principle of our constitution is that certain rights are given to the provinces and the residue remains with the federal govern-

ment; that is the distinction between our constitution and that of the United States.
Does the hon. gentleman contend that this parliament can create a company to build a dam all the way, across a navigable river?
Certainly not; but if this work can only be carried on by building a dam across the Pigeon river, it comes under subsection 10 of section 92, under which this parliament only has jurisdiction.
Just to connect the two ends.

My hon. friend tries to get around that, because, if I understand his argument, it is that the incorporators' should get power from the province of Ontario to build across the Ontario half of the river, and then get power from the State of Minnesota to build the other half, and then they would have to come here to get that ratified. He admits by his argument that the final jurisdiction over this work rests in this parliament. Then our friends say that we are interfering with the avowed policy of the province of Ontario. Personally I do not believe in public ownership. If the people of Ontario want their water-powers managed and controlled by the province, I have no quarrel with them; but I would like to know if the followers of the Ontario government go so far as to contend that all water-powers in the province, whether owned by the province or by private individuals, should he controlled and operated by the province. I cannot conceive that that is the policy of the Ontario government, otherwise they "would be taking away vested rights that must have existed for a hundred) years.
Those powers must he under some parliamentary jurisdiction. What other than the province?

I imagine that there are hundreds of water-powers in the province of Ontario which are being managed without a charter from anybody. The owners got the powers because they owned the land on which those powers are situated.
But the province could confiscate them.
Does my hon. friend say that the Ontario government has adopted as part of its policy the right to confiscate private property?
No, I do not say that they ought to confiscate it, but I say they have power to confiscate it if they chose to possess it.
I admit that they have power to confiscate anybody's private property, but is that their policy?
No.
My hon. friend says no, but they have done it.

When the Whitney government came into power, they found that a great many of these provincial rights had been given to private individuals, and they decided that they would reverse the policy of my hon. friend's party, and that in the future all these rights should be retained by the government for the people.
That policy was in vogue ten years before the Whitney government! came into power.

I am discussing whether it is the policy of the Ontario government, I will not say to confiscate, which is a harsh term, but to expropriate or acquire the private property of persons who happen to own water-powers. I am not discussing what the Ontario government did in the past; I am discussing what is their policy at the present time. The hon. member for Lincoln says that he understands that it is not their policy to confiscate or' expropriate the property of private parties. Then I understand that the whole burden of this discussion so far goes by the board, because it was based on the statement that there is a property here that belongs to the province of Ontario, and that this parliament ought not to interfere and take from the province a right which it enjoys. If we can believe the statements given by the hon. member and the telegrams read here this morning, we must conclude that the title to the six square miles, including this water-fall now under discussion, was granted in 1856 by a patent which extended down to the water's edge.

Will the hon. gentleman state whether in the evidence submitted or in the statement of the promoter of this Bill there is language to the effect that a water-power has been granted to this individual? I did not hear it.

I stated that the land- and I used the word in its broadest sense- the land facing on this river was granted by the province of Ontario in the year 1856 to a man named Stewart down to the water's edge.
That does not include the bed of the river.
It depends upon the stream.

I shall read the head note in this case. It applied to the Winnipeg river, which is a much larger river than the river under discussion. Here is the head note:
Where a grant of land is made bordering on a river, if a tidal river, the title to the bed is presumed to remain in the Crown, unless otherwise expressed in the grant; whereas if non-tidal, whether navigable or not, the title in the bed ad medium Slum aqus is presumed prima facie to be in the riparian proprietor.
Where, therefore, lands were granted by the Crown bounded by the Winnipeg river, a non-tidal river, the title to the bed of the river ad medium Slum aquae was held to have passed to the riparian owners by virtue of the grant to them, there being nothing in the grants, particulars of which are set out in the case, to rebut the presumption.
I do not think that my hon. friends will dispute that the Court oi Appeal there held that in the case of the Winnipeg river the title went right to the centre of the stream and, therefore, I think the same Court of Appeal would hold that the grant of land to the edge of the water on the Pigeon river would go to the centre of the stream.

Who owned the
water?
My hon. friend is not serious in that question.
Yes, I am quite serious. Who has the proprietary interest in the water?

It is an elementary principle of British common law, something the student learns before he takes his first examination, that the water belongs, for the time being, to the man over whose land it happens to be, subject to the rights of the public to navigation over it; and the owner, so long as he does not divert it and take it away, has a right to use it over his own land and turn it into the stream again so that the next riparian below him may have the use of it. Surely my hon. friend was not serious in asking for information on as elementary a matter of law as that. I contend that under this decision Stewart or his assignee is the absolute owner of that land out to the centre of the stream and the absolute owner of the use of that water so long as he does not divert it from the stream. If that is the case, the province of Ontario has no rights in this property or water-power, and, according to the admission of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), it is not the policy of the Ontario government to expropriate or take away from private parties the rights which they own, so they have not any intention of taking this water-power to themselves, and if they did they would have to pay the owners for it. Thus they have no right to say that we should not grant legislation allowing these people to utilize the water.
Coming to the question of expropriation, the amendments grant no right in regard to the Nipigon river beyond the right to establish pole lines. The right of expropriation is continued with regard to the Pigeon river. If I am correct in my assumption that this is not the property of the province of Ontario but of Stewart or his assigns the province of Ontario then has no legal right to come here and interfere unless this parliament lays down the principle that no man in Ontario has the right to own or look at a water-power except with the consent of the provincial government of Ontario. Coming from another province I am not prepared to assent to that, and I doubt if hon. gentlemen from other provinces are prepared. I am myself interested in a number of water-powers; my father was in the business before me and I presume other members in this House are similarly interested. I certainly will not subscribe to the doctrine that any province has a right to come in and take my property without my consent unless they pay me a pretty big fee. Considering that we have jurisdiction, considering that the province of Ontario does not own the land, considering that if this communicates with works going across the river we have the only jurisdiction, I think we are justified, not only justified but compelled if we are to be logical, to vote for this Bill and pass this legislation. Why should we go to Ontario and then in the end have this company come back here to have their works ratified?

The hon. gentleman has taken a few liberties with the House that perhaps it would be as well if he had not taken. He says that the property where it is proposed to work this water-power or erect a dam in connection with the power is private property belonging to a man named Stewart, or granted to him at a certain time. There is not the slightest evidence before this committee of this fact. The hon. gentleman who promotes this Bill has read a telegram from a certain authority in the parliament buildings at Toronto that simply says that in connection with a certain part of this river a certain grant was made in 1854. There is no evidence that the particular spot in the river mentioned in the telegram is the place where

this power plant is proposed to be erected. The Bill is wide open as to the right of selection which this company will have, as to where it will erect its power on this large stream. There is nothing in the Bill tying this company down to erecting its works at the point where it says it owns land. Now that the promoter says he proposes to erect the power works on the private property of this person Stewart, to whom it was granted in 1856, I assume that he will have no objection to having it specified in this Bill that his works are to be erected there and at no other place on this river. Then we will see where we are at and we will know that we are dealing with land owned by a private individual; but as a member of this committee I refuse to support or to allow to pass through unopposed, a noxious Bill that allows a company to make its own selection on the whole course of the river. I suppose my hon. friend who is promoting this Bill, will have no objection, in view of his own statement that the company are going to erect their works on this particular spot and not on Crown property or property expropriated from other people, to stipulate that in his Bill
Will my hon. friend accept the Bill provided I agree to his proposition? If he will, I will accept it.
No doubt the hon. gentleman would be very glad to get his Bill through on any terms at all.
Will my hon. friend kindly answer me?

If the hon. gentleman is going to get his Bill through-and it looks as if he were, from the attitude of the government-then it should specify where the works are to be erected. If we cannot get the Bill thrown out by the House, we must get for the people the best that we can.
My hon. friend who is promoting the Bill, must not ask us what we will do, in case he makes a certain proposition. Let him make his offer and then we will consider whether it is a proper one or not.

The hon. member from Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) seems to think it would be a fair proposition to say that this development should take place in the location mentioned in the vicinity of Pigeon River falls, mentioned in this telegram. I am willing to agree that the company should be tied down to a specific place and that the Bill should name that place. I know the locality. My telegram was sent to the registrar at Port Arthur asking him for the date of the patent of the land adjoining Pigeon River falls.

His reply was that the date of the patent was not known in his office, but the locality was the Stewart location and the plans showed that the rights of the patentee went to the water's edge. Then I wired to Toronto to have the records searched, and I have a reply stating that the Stewart location was deeded in 1856, so that we have perfect identification of the land as being at the Pigeon River Falls where the intention is to develop the power. There is no other point in the minds of the promoters, and I am quite willing to have that defined in the Bill, if that will meet the views of the hon. gentlemen.

The hon. gentleman is of course anxious to get some Bill, but the objection is that we have no right to interfere in this sort of legislation at all. The hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell) has shown the best reason why the Bill should be withdrawn; and as our advice has not been listened to, perhaps my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) will accept the logical results of the argument of the hon. member from Carleton. That hon. gentleman argued that because the property is privately owned, therefore the Dominion must assume jurisdiction over it.
I object to being quoted as having said something I did not say.

The logical result of the hon. member's argument was that we need not trouble any more about this, because the property, which runs to the water's edge, has passed into private hands, and therefore the province has no more control over it.
Yes.
My hon. friend will revise that opinion if he thinks it over. According to that the property I own in St. Catharines, the province of Ontario has no control over.
Does my hon. friend understand me to have said that because the property had passed into private control, the province of Ontario had no control over it?
That is what I understood.
The hon. gentleman is in error. The province of Ontario would have no legislative control over it unless they attempted to expropriate it or take it for their own use.

But they have legislative control over it because if property has passed from the province of Ontario to a private owner, it does not follow that

the province has still not the right to tax it or expropriate it.
How does this Bill interfere with any of those rights?

One at a time. Has not the province of Ontario still jurisdiction over property and civil rights in the province? The very fact that the title to that land has come down-and I am not admitting that it has-to the present private owner and that these works are going to be built there, is the very reason why this Dominion parliament has no right to exercise jurisdiction in the matter. These parties propose to build on property which is subject to taxation and expropriation and every other power the province has the right to exercise with regard to it.

Does my hon. friend say that if this Bill were to pass, and this company were incorporated, we would be taking away from Ontario the civil rights reserved to the province under the British North America Act?

I do not say so, but? that would be the result of my hon. friend's argument. He said that because private people owned this land, the Dominion parliament can do no harm in allowing this1 charter to go through. But we do not know what rights the province of Ontario may choose to exercise over this property. The hon. gentleman says we are not concerned with the past, but only the present policy of the Ontario government. Well, we are concerned with its present policy and its future policy as well, and we have no right to tie up by our legislation the hands of the Ontario government. Because the province has done nothing which would be an obstacle to our passing this Bill, are we to assume that it might not do something in future to which the passage of this Bill might be a hindrance ? I understand that the Ontario government has a policy which involves expropriation of these water-powers under certain conditions by a certain commission in compliance with certain rules, and we should not do anything here which would hamper the provincial government in the carrying out of that policy. I have not heard any one in this House declare what is the best policy for Ontario. What we have said is that the province of Ontario must be left alone to deal with this matter itself, and that we must not interfere with its power, past, present or future.

I think a word might be said with reference to the question interjected by the hon. member for Carleton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell) as to whether it would be possible, if this Act were passed, to interfere with the right of expropriation of the province of Ontario. I am inclined to think that it would materially effect all the Tights of the province in reference to that matter. The province of Ontario has enunciated a policy.
Does my hon. friend contend that the passing of this Bill would affect the legal rights of Ontario as to expropriation, or simply affect the policy of the Ontario government?

I compliment myself that I have a habit of making reasonably clear what I intend to say. I am inclined to think that if we pass this legislation we entirely hamper the action of the Ontario legislature.
From a legal standpoint?
From a legal, a moral and a physical standpoint, or any other you like. The policy of the Ontario government is to control its water-powers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What water-powers?

All water-powers in the province which are of advantage to the public in their locality. I do not think the word would apply to an ordinary mill pond. Any stream that is in the general interest of the public to develop, that would be a source of revenue to the province, of general advantage to the province, I think it is the policy of the Ontario government to control such rivers and streams. Now we have enunciated that policy, we have acted upon it, and in 1907 we passed an Act in reference to expropriations, where questions of this kind arise. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) asked, if we passed this legislation will it interfere with the right of the province to expropriate? Why, the foundation of expropriation is gone, we have given it to the member for Rainy River, instead of reserving it to the public.
After the member for Rainy River has exercised his rights of expropriation under this Bill, does my hon. friend then contend that the province of Ontario has not the right of expropriation?

I am going to show my hon. friend, if he will give me time. I was saying that in my opinion this Bill does interfere with the policy of the Ontario government, and with their Tight to expropriate. Has the hon. gentleman forgotten that this Bill, in its amended form, proposes to incorporate the provisions of the Electricity and Fluid Expropriation Act passed by this parliament in 1907? If we turn to the provisions of that Act we will find that not only is the export of electricity regulated by it, but if any one contravenes the provisions of that Act he is made subject to a penalty. The Ontario government

proaching the danger of creating a conflict between the provinces and the federal government? What is the wise policy? Is it a wise policy, using the words of the right hon. gentleman himself, to attempt by brute force to control the Ontario legislature? Is it wise, on the other hand, that we should not recognize that the province, in the interests of its people, have enunciated a policy, have set to work to carry out that policy, and in the development of that policy are now extending it year by year, and have done it in good faith, in the interest of the people? We are the federal head, and would it be wise for us to interfere with the rights of the province? For what? Why, the rights of the province for the sake of a speculative company, a company that does not profess to act in the interest of the people. If it did, I would have my doubts, I would have a mental reservation about it. But it does not profess to come here in the interests of the people. It comes year after year with dogged determination. Turned down two years ago, and turned down a year ago in the Senate, still this company crops up again with dogged pertinacity. 'Not in the interest of the people, but for the benefit of the speculator and the exploiter, not for the purpose of carrying power or light so much to the people of Ontario as for the purpose of exporting power, that great source of wealth, into a rival country, this company comes forward and asks for this right. Is it for that that we will invite a conflict between the elements of the Dominion, the provinces and the federal government, is it for that we will jeopardize the harmony that should prevail between the Dominion and the various provinces, is it for that that we shall say to a province :	'We will turn you down and ignore
your rights, your interests and your wishes? I say it is not wisdom, it is not statesmanship, and I hope that it is not what, in the end, this government will do.
I will be amazed and I will sincerely deplore it, entirely aside from political considerations, if the premier of this Dominion, at a time when he is finishing his work

Oh, oh.
Mr. LENNOX

very nearly finishing
it

Not quite so soon.
Mr. LENNOX

should so far forget what
is due to the provinces, what is due to himself, what is due to Canada, as to say that we will turn down a province for the sake of a speculative company. Surely there never was a better opportunity for the right hon. gentleman, who says that he has had several opportunities of distinguishing himself, to distinguish himself still more and to signalize his real adherence to what

used to be a very old war cry of the Liberal party-provincial rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the blandishments with which my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has so kindly referred to me, I must tell him, as I have had occasion to say many times to my Conservative friends, that when they talk of provincial rights they talk of a subject upon which they have very little knowledge, and whatever love they have for it is of very recent importation. There was a time when they ignored provincial rights. I welcome their conversion and I rejoice that they now recognize the error of their ways. We are all at one upon the question of provincial rights. But if it is not fair, if it is not conducive to harmony that the Dominion government should invade the rights of the provinces, neither would it be conducive to harmony that the provinces should invade the rights of the Dominion. The province of Ontario have a policy, and it is the preservation of their water-powers. With regard to their water-powers what right can the province of Ontario claim? If I hold from the province of Ontario 200 acres of land in one of the northern townships, in Algoma or Thunder Bay, if there is a stream or a water-power upon that land have the province of Ontario power to take that away from me? I do not think they have. They have undoubtedly the right of eminent domain and could take it away from me by expropriation. But that is not what I understand to be the policy of the Ontario government today. Nor do I understand that the Ontario government contemplates taking away water-powers which may be on such land. What I understand the Ontario government want to do is to keep in their own hands water-powers on their own Crown lands. That is the policy which they adopted, and properly so. I commend them for it. My hon. friend says, however, that we want to control the rights of the provinces on navigable streams. Well, that is perhaps a doubtful power, but as far as I am concerned I said to mv hon. friend the promoter of this Bill (Mr. Conmee) the other day that he should not attempt to exercise power on the Nipigon river, that there is a conflict between ourselves and the province of Ontario, and as I am a great believer in provincial rights, much more so than those recent converts on the other side of the House who seek to champion the rights of the provinces, I asked him to eliminate that portion of the Bill and he did so. But, when we come to the Pigeon river we have to deal with the case of an international stream. To whom should the power belong to control the waters of an international stream? I have
not had the opportunity for a very long time of knowing personally the hon. member for Portage La Prairie (Mr. Meighen) but he seems to be endowed with a logical mind, although I believe he has not quite apprehended the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice on this subject. He said that the Minister of Justice had imported into this debate an element which should, properly speaking, have nothing to do with it, that is to say that the Minister of Justice claimed that we had jurisdiction to deal with this Bill because it allowed the exportation of electrical energy to the other side of the border line. I have not read the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice to-day, but I would observe to my hon. friend from Portage La Prairie that the exportation of electrical energy is not carried on in the same way as would be the exportation of wheat, oats or any other commodity. There is only one way by which electrical energy can be exported from one country to another, and that is by works from one side of the boundary to the other.
What works are necessary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There must be a wire from one part of the country to the other.
How do they distribute it all over Canada and attach it to houses?
By wires and cables.
No, in cans and by wagon loads.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks that we export electrical energy in cans, I would tell him that that means of exportation is altogether inadequate.
What I said was in answer to the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister that there was only one way in which it could be exported.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By this Bill?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly. I know my hon. friend from Rainy River too well to believe that he will undertake to export electrical energy by cans. He has bigger ideas than that. He wants to do a work of an international character. Upon that question the jurisdiction remains with this House, and my hon. friend from South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) will surely agree with me that it is right, proper and conducive to harmony that the Dominion and not the province should exercise jurisdiction.

I do not know whether I may touch on some questions that others have already dealt with



Sir WILFRID _LAURIER. Dear me, I thought everything had been touched upon in this debate.

But notwithstanding that, I have my views upon the question and therefore the right to present them. This is not the first time that there seems to have been a conflict of jurisdiction between the provinces and the federal authority. We have had many such conflicts in regard to which cases have been taken to the courts and carried to the highest court in the empire. In each case where a finality was reached there was a decision in favour of one side or the other. That has, to some extent, accentuated the feeling on this question in regard to who owns and who should control these rights. The provinces have become somewhat sensitive upon the question and are growing more and more so every year, especially in view of the fact that there are inroads being made upon their rights almost every year by legislation put through the federal parliament. We have had several contests between the provinces and the Dominion and invariably the provinces came off best. At one time it was claimed that the timber on certain lands belonged to the Dominion, but that claim failed before the tribunals of the land. At one time it was claimed that the federal authority had the right to control the minerals, but the decision was that all the minerals except gold and silver belonged to the provinces. Again, the Dominion asserted control over the fisheries, but the decision was that while the Dominion could control the mode of catching fish and declare what should be a close season and what should be an open season, yet the right in the fish themselves belonged to the provinces and that, while the province could not delimit where the license-holder should work, yet the province had power to issue licenses, and to-day the province of Ontario can issue licenses to fish in the Georgian bay, or in Lake Superior, or any of the inland waters. The question as to jurisdiction over streams was carried to the Privy Council, and the right of the provinces in the streams was established. Is it not the streams that make the water-powers, and I have no doubt the decisions of the courts will be that the water-powers should be controlled by the province. Up to the present time we have never had the contention raised that the water-powers belonged to any other authority than the provinces, but now it is said that this parliament has the power to incorporate a company to utilize these water-powers and to take their control away from the provinces. In future, it is to be laid down, that companies which get their entity from the federal parliament will be able to supplant the provinces in these rights. I venture to think that if the time should come when this question will be fought out in the highest court of the empire, the de-

cision will be that the province of Ontario is supreme.
In pursuance of their undoubted right the province of Ontario has established a Hydro-electric Power Commission and that commission has entered into contracts to sell power to municipalities and to manufacturers and to others who desire to use electricity. The Ontario government hope to develop a large part of that electricity from the latent water-powers that belong to the province and which it is their intention to develop. It is said by those who have given the subject attention that there are water-powers enough in the province of Ontario to turn every spindle in every machine, to keep every factory running, to light every town and village and city, to supply every manufacturer with motive power and all the farmers with power to run their threshing machines and to light their residences and barns. The policy of the Ontario government is to utilize that power and to regulate it so that justice may be done to all and injustice to none. But the object of this company which we are asked now to incorporate is to invade the sacred rights of the province and to interfere with their policy in that respect. Is this parliament to be a party to allowing this company to dispoil the province of what belongs to it. This question of federal and provincial rights is a burning question in the different provinces, and if this government continues its policy of interfering with provincial rights the time may come and undoubtedly will come when a bitter fight will arise between the provinces and the federal authority. In the United States interference by the federal authority with state rights led to the secession of many of the states from the Union. Who knows that we will not bring about the same condition of affairs in this Dominion if this parliament year after year pursues the policy of invading the rights of the provinces. The present government by its improper interference, and I say it advisedly, with the rights of Manitoba, has almost driven Manitoba into revolt against federal authority. The province of Manitoba sent to this parliament a majority of members opposed to the government because the government has interfered with her undoubted Tights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When was
that ?

With regard to the extension of the provincial boundaries, with regard to the educational rights of the province, and with regard to other things, the result of which has been to create in Manitoba a distinctly unfriendly feeling against the Dominion government. The same thing has occurred in British Columbia. The absolute refusal of this government to submit the claims of that province to a competent and independent tribunal, and in-

terference with the province on the question as to who shall have the right to occupy her territory, has almost driven British Columbia into a revolt against the federal authorities and a large majority of the representatives from that province have been sent here to oppose this government. Notwithstanding that experience in the case of these two very important provinces, this government seems anxious to invite the antagonism of the great province of Ontario by depriving her of authority which she has the right to exercise. I say that this government is driving Ontario as well into revolt, and if this insane policy is pursued it will not be long before the present government will find that Ontario will be as solidly arrayed against them as are British Columbia and Manitoba. The conduct of the government is inviting this contest. It is said that if you tread on a worm it will turn, and I say that this government is tramping on an authority that is too great and too powerful not to be reckoned with in the future. If the government continues this fatuous policy in the interest of speculators or spoilators, I do not care which you call them, there is a threatening day coming when rupture will result and when the Dominion of Canada as a federation will suffer. I warn them that they are treading upon dangerous ground, and the premier would be well advised if he would call off his friends who are driving this on regardless of all consequences, knowing that t.hev are dealing with what the province believes to be its undoubted right.

Just a word to put my hon. and learned friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) right on one or two points. Extreme zeal to advance the interests of his desk mate has carried him a little beyond the legal position he attempted to maintain. The hon. gentleman was not in his seat this morning, or he would have heard the answer I made to the statement that the fact that the ground came down to the water's edge gave this grantee the entire area, because, as I pointed out, in the grant from the Crown there is a reservation of at least five per cent for roads and highways, out of which the Crown could make its own selection anywhere it chose on this property.

Is my hon. friend aware that it has been stated by the hon. member for Rainy River that that option had been exercised and that the Surveyor General of Ontario told him that the Crown could not go any further?

The hon. member for Rainy River made no statement further than this, that certain areas had been opened up on this property, but he did not make the statement that the Crown had exercised that five per cent provision.

The hon. member evidently did not catch my words. I gave the circumstances under which the Crown was called upon to exercise its right of laying out public roads and utilizing the five per cent reserve in the patent, and I pointed out that they had made two main roads from which one or two branches went to the water's edge. They were requested to make other roads, and the answer of the Minister of Crown Lands, the Hon. Mr. Gibson, was that the Crown had exercised its right because it had utilized the five per cent reserve.
I accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but I would like to know if he has ever heard that it was not that five per cent that was used.
It could not be any other.

In the second place, the hon. member for Carleton laid great emphasis on the case of the Keewatin Power Company against the town of Ken-ora; the hon. member for South Essex, (Mr. A. H. Clarke) also referred to that case. In reading the case carefully, both of these hon. gentlemen will observe that it merely decides that in the case of ordinary rivers flowing through the country, the presumption is that the bed of the stream to the middle of the stream is vested in the patentee from the Crown. That is only a presumption liable to be rebutted by evidence or practice. But it does not apply to the case of an international river. Chief Justice Moss, in giving his judgment, said :
But in this case we are not dealing with the great lakes nor with a river forming part of the international boundary.
And so on through the whole case. Rivers forming the international boundary are especially excepted from the consideration of this case. So the whole argument of my hon. friend from Carleton is just as good as if it had never been made.

When this matter was before the Private Bills Committee, the Ontario government sent a special representative here to present their views. Notwithstanding the statement that was made on behalf of the Ontario government, the committee adopted the Bill as introduced, with all the objections which my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) has since ventured to suggest should be removed. Therefore I think it only fair that the Ontario government should have another opportunity of appearing before the committee. Surely my hon. friend will not say, after having ignored altogether the representations of the Ontario government, as presented so well by Mr. Black-stock, that it is fair to the Ontario govern-

ment that this Bill should be pressed through the House without that government having another opportunity to be heard. I appeal to the Prime Minister to say whether that is fair as a champion of provincial rights. Those of us who come from the province of Ontario are specially interested in this matter. We heard the right hon. gentleman's party for many years in the province of Ontario claiming to be the only champions of provincial rights. While they were doing that, they were taking care of the rights of their own supporters. While professing to fight for the rights of the people of Ontario, they were granting special rights to their own supporters in that province. They took the ground at one time that timber in the province of Ontario applied for by people in the United States could be taken across to the United States and cut into lumber there, and while doing that they were championing provincial rights. " That matter was brought up in the legislature by the Liberal Conservative party while my hon. friend was there, and the Liberal Conservative party took the ground that the timber should not be taken out of the province and cut into lumber in the United States, but should be cut into lumber in Ontario, and my hon. friend voted against that resolution when it was introduced into the Ontario legislature. That question was fought out between the two parties in the province and when the people understood what the policy of the Liberal Conservative party was on that question, the legislature was compelled to adopt it, and the timber was no longer allowed to be taken to the United States to be cut into lumber, but was required to be cut into lumber in the province of Ontario. However, that is beside the question. I only point this out in answer to the Prime Minister and to remind the Minister of Railways who was then in the legislature and was also a noted champion of provincial rights.
My hon. friend's history is all wrong.
Oh no, it is not. Will miy hon. friend deny that the policy of compelling the manufacture of timber into lumber in Ontario was first introduced by the Conservative party.
What timber?
Crown timber. I challenge the Minister of Railways to deny that statement.
If my hon. friend will study the case he will find that it was Mr. Miseampbell who under certain circumstances introduced a resolution in the legislature and not Mr. Meredith.
Long after Mr. Meredith left the House.

It was a resolution introduced in the House under particular circumstances which was voted down as many others are. The Liberal party took up the question some time later and put on the statute-book an Act which compelled the sawing of logs in this country.

I will accept that state-' ment. The Liberal party put it on the statute book, but year after year they allowed the timber to go out of the province, and according to the admission of the hon. gentleman it was a conservative and not a Libera] who first introduced that policy in the Ontario House. The policy was adopted by the Liberals of Ontario under pressure of the Conservatives.
Nonsense.
My hon. friend knows that very well.
No, I deny that. It was a subject of discussion for many years before that.
I suppose he will deny that his party were granting special rights to his friends, such as timber limits to Captain Sullivan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The clause before the committee is clause No. I. It allows a great deal of latitude in discussion and I am not disposed to prevent that, but any argument used by the hon. gentleman must be applied to clause I in some way and matters brought before the House must not be discussed for themselves alone unless in relation to this clause.
I bow to the Chairman, I am only answering the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In discussing Mr. Miseampbell you are missing the point.
The right hon. gentleman introduced the question of the policy of the two parties on provincial rights and I was answering that point.
You did not answer it very well.

I do not wish to carry it) further; my point is that it would be fair for this committee to return the corrected. Bill to the Private Bills Committee for their consideration, so that the Ontario government might have an opportunity to have their representative present and give their views upon this Bill. This is undoubtedly an interference with the policy of the provincial government of Ontario. The very changes that have been made in the Bill since its first introduction show that. I

am quite sure the Prime Minister wishes to be fair with this House and with the province of Ontario, and that he would not be a party to pressing through the House a Bill, of this kind without first giving the province an opportunity to appear before, the Private Bills Committee, for the amended Bill has not been before that committee. This House should not adopt a Bill of this kind which is taking away the rights of the people of Ontario and conferring them on a speculative concern.

From the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite it appears that the claim of jurisdiction of this parliament to enact this legislation is based very largely on the theory that the power we are giving to this company to export their product to the United States, gives exclusive jurisdiction to this parliament. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), the Minister of Justice, and the Prime Minister have taken that view. As a matter of reason I do not think it was intended by the British North America Act that jurisdiction should be given to this parliament by the mere fact that we put into a Bill the right to do something which we ouselves cannot enforce, and which the persons to whom we give that right cannot do. Our saying that this company may export their power to the United States does not give them the right to go into the United States and carry on that exportation and we ourselves cannot compel them to do what they say they have the right to do. In other words we cannot give any more legal authority to this company to export into the United States than can the province of Ontario. The right hon. gentleman says that because this company may incidentally require to erect some poles and lines beyond the limits of Ontario and in a foreign country that fact in itself gives power to this parliament. The right hon. gentleman will agree that if a railroad company authorized by a provincial legislature to build a railway which is intended to go into the State of Maine can give that company authority to build that railway, that is a much stronger case than the case of simply allowing transportation lines to be built into the United States to export power. I quote a case on that point. In the province of New Brunswick 6ome years ago power was given by the provincial legislature to a railway company to commence and build a railroad in the province of New Brunswick, the intention being that it would be extended on into the -state of Maine. It was extended on into the state of Maine and the company obtained corporate authority from the legislative assembly of Maine to build and did build a section of that railway in that state. A shareholder, in an action, set up
the plea that the provincial legislature had no right to grant that authority to that railway because it was a railway extending to a foreign country and the question came up on that direct issue: had the provincial legislature power to incorporate that company, knowing it was going to extend its railway into Maine. The Court answered the question in this way:
The fact of the legislature of a foreign country authorizing the construction of a line of railway in that country for the purpose of connecting with a provincial railway does not in any way affect the authority of the legislature of the province to legislate with respect to the railway within the bounds of the province.
We cannot legislate for a foreign country, and the fact that authority to extend transmission lines in the United States of America, is mentioned in this Bill, would not prevent the parliament of Ontario from granting to this company all the rights, powers, and privileges which they could enjoy within the province of Ontario. If you are asking for the power to transmit your electricity from one province to another, the jurisdiction would be in this parliament, but we have not jurisdiction in the case of transmission from a province to a foreign countrv. If my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) will look at the wording of the subsection he quotes, namely, 'Local works of the provinces other than such, are of the following class,'-that is to say all local works are within the exclusive jurisdiction of Ontario except the following classes-
Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other portions of the province or extending beyond the limits of the province.
The words 'extending beyond the limits of the province,' I take it, mean extending into some unorganized district, because this Act was passed in 1867 and there were other territories then within the Dominion, outside the provinces, so that the exception was intended to apply to cases where you would extend your railway into some unorganized district, but not into some foreign country. Take the next exception:
Lines of steamships between the provinces and any British or foreign country.
That would apply to a line running into the United States, which the province would have no right to authorize.
There was a proposition made by hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) a few moments ago which has not received the attention it deserved, and that is that this is practically a new Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I know there are some people who do not realize what that means. If it were a new Bill, shorn of all its objectionable features, we could understand that it would not probably be necessary to give the Ontario government an opportunity of presenting their views upon it before a committee of this House. But this new Bill not only eliminates certain features, but is introducing others. According to the notice of the amendments which we had, it is provided that we shall incorporate the whole of this Electrical Expropriation Bill 'which was passed in 1897, and it is therefore just as important, as before, that the government of Ontario should have the opportunity of being heard with regard to it. It embodies provisions	just as
dangerous, even more so than those we had in the old Bill. The Ontario government are the best judges of what seriously affects that province.	Whether
our hon. friends opposite like it or not, people of Ontario have, by an overwhelming majority, committed their affairs to the keeping of Sir James Whitney and his cabinet; and these representatives have the right to be heard. When the first Bill was introduced the hon. gentleman who is promoting it, said it was all right in every particular, just as emphatically as he is now doing in the case of the present Bill. That first Bill having been bowled out on the 19th of last month, he now comes with an entirely new proposition, thereby admitting that he was wrong then. Well, I am strongly of the opinion that he is equally wrong now. We have the statement of the Prime Minister, not two weeks old, that he will respect the rights of the provinces, but he has abandoned that position to-day. Surely it is only right when the progressive policy of the Ontario government with respect to water-powers is being invaded, as it is by this measure, that the government should have the Tight to appear before this parliament or in committee and state its case. Ontario, besides being one of the old and large provinces, is the province which stood the brunt of the fight for provincial rights; and after having established its rights as a province through a long series of litigation; it comes now and asks that this parliament shall not, now pass a measure, such as this, which infringes on those rights. My hon. friend says he is a champion of provincial rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not wish to rob him of any of his laurels and I should be sorry to see him cast any shadow upon his reputation in that regard, but whoever may have fought most gallantly for provincial rights, it was the province of Ontario that waged the battle.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
It was the province of Ontario that won the fight, and it is the province of Ontario, of which my hon.
friend of Thunder Bay is a distinguished representative in this House, whose rights are threatened now. To-day it is Ontario, to-morrow it may be British Columbia or Quebec. Let the right hon. gentleman who leads this House recollect that this is a question in which both provincial and federal rights are concerned. Again I say that if we are going to develop Canada we can only do it by seeing that the rights of every portion of the Dominion are respected, not only their rights but their prejudices, and so far as possible, the will of every part of the Dominion. We are to-day at a critical point in our history. I am convinced that no more dangerous question comes before this House than the question of provincial rights. Look at the geographical position of this country, see how diverse are the interests of Canada, and do not shut your eyes to the fact that there is dissatisfaction in many of the provinces to-day at the action of the government. Day after day the friction increases, and some day it will reach such a point that the strain can no longer be endured, and we shall see some of the provinces wishing to get out of the confederation in which they cannot have due recognition of their rights. I do not think it will be Ontario. I do not think it will be Quebec; I think the greater danger is in regard to the western provinces. I urge again on the Prime Minister not to ignore the appeal of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain). Do not throw this objection aside with a wave of the hand, saying, I have great respect for committees which send these Bills before us. In this case that argument does not apply. The Bill now before us is, practicaly, a new Bill, it is practically new legislation, adopting a new principle, and is it fair that the government and the people of Ontario should be excluded from an opportunity of appearing before this parliament and presenting their views?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is quite true that it was the province of Ontario which fought the battle of provincial rights, and it is quite true that my hon. friend did not help very much in that battle. It is also true that he and his friends were against us in that battle, and the glory of the victory belongs to the Liberals of the province of Ontario. But my hon. friend is welcome to his tardy conversion, and after delivering to us an eloquent speech he has ended with the old refrain, Ontario, Ontario. My hon. friend says that I should give some heed to the request made by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain). If I did not heed the request of the hon.

member for Peel, it was not through discourtesy for that hon. member. My hon. friend says we have a new Bill to-day. It is true we have a new Bill, but the old Bill has been amended to meet the requests of the representatives of the Ontario government who were before the committee.
The Ontario government still objects to the Bill, notwithstanding the amendments and changes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does the Ontario government object, for instance, to this second section of the Bill:
The works authorized by this Act are declared to he works for the general advantage of Canada.
I understand that Mr. Blackstock took strong objection to that. Does my hon. friend say that the government of Ontario want those clauses restored now?
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then the government of Ontario objected to the powers of expropriation being taken away in regard to the Nipigon river. Does my hon. friend want those to be restored also? In fact, the Bill has been amended in the line desired by the province in everything, and I am not sure that we shall not also agree to the request of the province when we come to consider the power of expropriation as regards the Pigeon river. This is the only question before us, and when we come to the power of expropriation on the Pigeon river, we shall see whether or not the rights of the province are being infringed upon. If the Tights of the province in the Pigeon river are being infringed upon, we will consider that matter when we come to it, and I will see whether I am able to support my hon. friend.

The right hon. gentleman has asked whether I object to clause number two declaring that the work authorized bv this Act are works for the general advantage of Canada.
