In addition to the foregoing notices, which were published in accordance with the requirements of rule 90, sections 1, B 2 and C 2, your committee find that the following circular as well as a copy of the Bill as amended by the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce, were mailed to each of the participating policy-holders of the company in Canada, Newfoundland, Great Britain and Ireland and the United States, between the 29th day of March, 1909, and the 6th day of April, 1909, in the manner set forth in the declaration of Alexander Gillespie hereto attached.
Then the report gives a copy of a letter addressed to the participating policy-holders by John Hoskin, vice-president of the company, and also a copy ot a letter or certificate by A. G. Ramsay in reference to the intention of the company when the Act of 1879 was being applied for. It also contained a declaration of Mr. Alexander Gillespie as to the mailing of the copies of the Bill and the copies of these letters. My reason for asking that this Bill be referred back to the Committee on Standing Orders is the fact that no declaration, has yet been made, either by the examiner of private Bills or the Committee on Standing Orders, as to whether these notices were sufficient for the purpose or not. I need not read or refer to the rules of this House concerning the notices required io be given. All the members of this House are familiar with the fact that notice must be given and that a reference must be made either to the examiner of private Bills or the Committee on Standing Orders to inform this House whether or not these notices are sufficient for the purpose of the Bill. I might here remark that it is alleged that thirty years ago an error was made in the legislation that took place, and I submit that it would not be wise for this House now in dealing with this Bill to commit what I regard as a manifest error in overlooking the important requirements of the House in regard to the notice and the character of the notice. I submit that as a fair proposition, and I would say that it would be wise for us to refer the Bill back and get a report from the Standing Orders Committee as to whether these notices were sufficient or not.
But, I have another matter to which I desire to refer for a moment. We have this afternoon been discussing the question of provincial rights. There is no doubt that the provinces have a good deal to say with reference to policies of insurance. I believe that the Privy Council has held in a considered judgment, or perhaps in con-

sidered judgments, that an insurance policy comes within 'the words 'property and civil rights-.' Property and civil rights, we must all admit, must be dealt with by the provincial legislatures, and therefore, in addition to any notices that have been given, I submit that notices should be sent to every province in the Dominion of Canada where policies of insurance are held. I desire now to read an order in council that was passed by the Ontario government only a few days ago. I regard it as a very important protest from that government, and I shall place it on 'Hansard' so that every member of the House will be able to read it for himself and have ndtiee of its contents:
Copy of an order in council approved by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor the thirtieth day of April, A.D. 1909. The committee advise that the annexed report of the honourable the Attorney General with reference to the Bill respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company now before the Dominion parliament be approved of by Your Honour and that a despatch be forwarded to the Secretary of State, Ottawa, accompanied by a copy of the said report for the information of the government of the Dominion of Canada.
Certified, S. Lonsdale Capreol, clerk, Executive Council .
I am privately advised that a copy of this order in council was on Saturday last sent to a member of this government, presumedly the Secretary of State, so that I have no doubt the government are now in possession of it, and in all probability may have considered its contents. The order in council reads:
To His Honour the Lieutenant Governor in Council:-
The undersigned has had under consideration the Bill respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company now before the Dominion parliament and respectfully recommends that a despatch he forwarded to the Secretary of State, Ottawa, regarding the said Bill to the following effect:-
The Bill now before parliament regarding the Canada Life Assurance Company, if it becomes law will in effect alter the contract of every policy-holder on the participation plan and largely reduce the amount that he is legally entitled to out of the profits under the existing law. The extent to which such policy-holder will suffer if the Act is passed will be very greatly increased by the action of the directors and their shareholders in having unnecessarily increased the amount of the paid up capital stock from $125,000 to $1,000,000 (see the report of the Royal Commission as to this). An opinion with regard to the law has been obtained by some policyholders from Sir Robert Findlay. It is his opinion that the payments of dividends to the shareholders since 1879 in excess of 10 per cent of the profits of the business of the company have been ultra vires, there being
in his opinion no ground for the contention that the' shareholders are entitled to interest on capital and also to ten per cent of the profits, or to a sufficient part thereof to make up $80,000 a year to be paid them as dividends.
A large number of the policy-holders in the oompany reside in the province and their property and civil rights which are within the jurisdiction of this province would be interfered with by such legislation as is proposed in the present instance. The Bill having only recently passed the Standing Orders Committee, there is not sufficient time now that the session is approaching its close to fully consider the matter, and it is respectfully submitted that the government should procure the postponement of the consideration of the Bill until next session. The rights and the jurisdiction of the province are involved and ample time should be given to the provinces of the Dominion to consider the matter and decide what course should be adopted by them.
It also appears that many of the matters involved in another Bill ((the Life Insurance Bill) now before the House of Commons deal with matters within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province, as it is respectfully submitted that this Bill should also not become law during the present session.
(Signed) J. J. FOY, Attorney General.
Toronto, 30th April, ,1909.
In view of what the Minister of Finance said only a few moments ago I think I can make an appeal to him to pursue in the case of this Bill a course similar to that which he advised in reference to the Michigan Power Company Bill. I submit that this Bill which we are now considering be deferred, that it should not be proceeded with hastily, and that an opportunity should be given to the government of Ontario to be heard. I do not know any better way to enable a representative of the Ontario government to be heard than to refer this Bill back to the Standing Orders Committee, to notify the Ontario government of the day on which that committee will meet, and allow its representative to appear and enter a protest along the lines of the order in council which I have read.
I think this is a reasonable proposition. I therefore submit this motion to you, Mr. Speaker, in the confidence that the government will give it fair consideration, that they will permit all parties to be heard, and that they will not do anything hastily. I am only now dealing with the point as to referring the Bill back to the Committee on Standing Orders in order that it may be dealt with in the usual way.

I submit that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) has shown no reason why this Bill should be referred back to the Committee on Standing Orders. His argument that it should be so referred in order to have the question determined whether the province of Ontario or the Do-

minion has jurisdiction in the matter, is rather a strange one.

I trust the hon. gentleman does not desire to misrepresent me. I certainly stated as plainly as I could that this Bill had only been dealt with by the Standing Order Committee to the extent of preparing a list of the notices. But the committee in no way gave an opinion as to the sufficiency of these notices and I asked that the Bill be sent back to enable the committee to deal with it in that respect.

One reason given by my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) for referring hack the Bill was that the committee might consider whether or not sufficient notice had been given, and the other reason given by him was that an order in council had been passed by the Ontario government in reference to the Bill. 1 now understand my hon. friend to say that he does not set up that order in council as a reason why the Bill should be referred back, and if that is so I will have nothing more to say on that point.
If the Ontario government or the policy-holders, or the members of this House, desired to say whether or not they had sufficient notice, it would give them that opportunity.

No person knows better than my hon. friend whether or not the notice contemplated by the rules has been given or not, and I am surprised at this stage of the session, when every per-on wants to get away, when this Bill has already been twice referred to the Standing Orders Committee, and when it has been before this House for two months, that my hon. friend desired to again retard the passage of the Bill by having it referred back to the Standing Orders Committee. He has not pointed out a single irregularity in the notice. He is a member of the Standing Orders Committee, and he knows well whether or not the notice waB sufficient. It seems to me that there has never been before the House a Bill in regard to which more care has been taken to give public notice, or in which the rules of the House have been more fully complied with.

Does the hon. member regard the rules of the House as having been complied with when the Standing Orders Committee has reported to this House without saying whether or not the notices were according to the requirements? They have not reported that they examined the Bill and find that the notices have been ample. So that their report is equivalent to no report at all.

The Standing Orders Committee have reported exactly what Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
this House asked them to report, nothing more nor less. It is not the duty of the Standing Orders Committee, in the first instance, to report whether or not the notices aTe sufficient.
It is the duty of that committee to report whether the notices are sufficient or not.

I would be very glad if my hon. friend, when he speaks of the duty of a committee, would refer to some authority other than his own ipse dixit. 1 do not find that the rules require that. Rule 95 says:
Petitions for private Bills, when received by the House, are to be taken into consideration by the examiner, who shall report to the House in each case the extent to which the requirements of the rules regarding notices have been complied with.
When that is done in the case of any Private Bill, it is put on the Order Paper. A Bill does not go to the Standing Orders Committee at all unless the examiner finds that the rules have not been complied with. In this particular case, the examiner, who is an officer of great experience, found that the rules had been complied with, and so reported to the House. Therefore the Bill came properly before the House and was placed on the Order Paper. Some hon. gentlemen then said that in their opinion the notice was not sufficient, not because it was not inserted in a sufficient number of newspapers or a sufficient number of times, but because the notice relating to some section of the Bill was not sufficiently full to have made the policy-holders and others acquainted with the exact nature of the Bill. Therefore the House sent the Bill back to the Standing Orders Committee, and that committee reported that in their judgment the notice regarding a certain section of the Bill was not sufficient. Thereupon a new notice was given, and the Bill was then sent back to the Committee on Standing Orders to report what had been done. That committee has reported that the notice was inserted for five weeks in the ' Canada Gazette,' and in the newspapers, and was sent to every participating policy-holder in Canada, the United States and Newfoundland, and that copies of it were sent to England to be transmitted to every policy-holder there. I would like the hon. member for Halton to suggest what notice ought to have been given that has not been given.

What I said was that the Standing Orders Committee has not reported to the House whether the notices have been sufficient or not. It has expressed no opinion to guide the House, and my own impression is that the notices have not been sufficient. I do not want to discuss that now, because I think the Com-

mittee on Standing Orders is the proper place to discuss it. But my hon. friend will find that if he is going to proceed with a Bill asking for retroactive legislation, there has been no notice to that effect.

The committee has reported to this House what the House asked it to report. It did not ask the committee to report whether the notices were sufficient or not; it simply asked it to report what notices were given. The committee has done that. The rules of the House say what notice shall be required-five weeks in the ' Canada Gazette,' and one other newspaper at the place of the head office. The committee reports that that has_ been done. 1 do not understand that there is any complaint about the particularity of the notice in regard to clause 2 of the Bill which says:
Declaring that, in accordance with the uniform practice of the company, the profits in which the participating policy-holders are entitled to share are those realized from the company's life insurance business, exclusive of the interest earned on paid-up capital and on other moneys at the credit of the shareholders arising from interest so earned or from the shareholders' proportion of profits.
I think no hon. member will say that that is not full notice, indicating clearly what that particular section of the Bill was to be.
Could my hon. friend give us the exact language of the House in referring the Bill to the Committee?

I have not the page before me, but I remember quite well what it was. It referred the Bill back to report what notice had been given. I submit that we have abundant evidence of ample notice having been given. Therefore it is child's play to refer the Bill back to the Committee at this stage.

I do not think the hon. member who is usually pretty fair, has correctly apprehended or presented what the hon. member for Halton contends for. It is this, if I understand him rightly, that a certain duty is cast upon the Standing Orders Committee, and that duty has not been discharged, and by reason of that the matter should be referred back in order that they should report Jin accordance with the standing rules and orders of the House. Incidentally and very properly the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) pointed out that the manner in which the Standing Orders Committee discharge their duty is not a trivial or unimportant matter but a matter of great importance to the people generally. I am not inquiring as to whether or not they are to blame, but I am rather inclined to think they are not. That is not of so much concern as whether everything has been done that will safeguard the interests of the policy-holders who are so
extremely concerned in this matter. The rule as stated by Bourinot at page 749 is:
Under rule 53 of the Senate and Commons,
' petitions for private Bills, when received by the House, are to be taken into consideration (without special reference) _ by the Committee on Standing Orders, which is to report in. each case whether the rule_ with regard to notice has been complied with.'
I am not losing sight of the fact that we have modified the rules since this was written. But under our present rules, when a matter of this kind is referred to that committee, then the rule as here laid down by Bourinot applies. Under the present rule these petitions do not go to the Standing Orders Committee if favourably reported on by the Examiner of Petitions for Private Bills, and in this case that officer reported that everything required for public safety in reference to a Bill of this kind had been complied with. In this way the Bill came before this House and was referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce where it was investigated. It was only when it came back to this House that attention was called to the inadequacy of the advertisement in reference to section 2 and the absence of advertisement with reference to sections 4 and 5. The House then referred the Bill back to the Standing Orders Committee on the 22nd of March. The item in the votes and proceedings is:
On motion of Mr. Sharpe (Ontario), it was ordered, that the order made this day for further consideration in Committee of the Whole of Bill (No. 56) An Act respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company, be discharged, and that the said Bill be referred to the Select 'Standing Committee on Standing Orders for further consideration as to the efficiency of the notices given therefor.
That is what the Standing Orders Committee is for, not to report to us as to the facts which come before it, because we can consider those facts as well as they can, but to consider whether or not, as a matter of procedure and of law and justice the notices, which have been given are sufficient. We were then beginning to get on the right track through the efforts and the astuteness of the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and on March 25 we find this in the Votes and Proceedings:
Mr. McCraney, from the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders, presented the third report of the said committee, which is as follows:-
Pursuant to the order of the House of the 22nd instant, your committee have considered Bill (No. 56) respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company, as reprinted and amended by the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce, and find:

Now you will see what the duty of the Standing Committee is, and they recognized it at this time when they reported back to the House.
That sections 1 and 3 are clearly within the terms of the notice as published.
That is they give their findings as a court, they give their judgment and find that sections 1 and 3 were within the notice.
2.	That the wording of the notice does not sufficiently indicate the nature of the powers to be granted under section 2.
That was the important section, so that down to that point you have it that there had not been sufficient notice of what the company were applying for under their very important section No. 2, and
3.	That sections 4 and 5 are not mentioned in either the notice or the petition. .
Thus we have the rule I have read, we have the recognition of that rule in the order made on March 22, and again in the report made on March 25. Thus from the time that the hon. member for North Ontario took it in hand until March 25, the matter was regular, it was getting on the right track again but it went wrong again and the next proceeding, I am sorry to say, was on motion of my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke), and I must say that although it was not noticed at the time, probably this led to the difficulty we are in now, not of course intentionally, but I would suggest to my hon. friend that since he got us into this difficulty he is in duty bound to try and get us out of it again. His motion speaks for itself. We know that in tne meantime certain advertisements had been printed and certain steps taken to publish what it was then said was the object of the company. I am not prepared to admit that this notice was in any shape sufficient. A colorable notice, a notice calculated to lull and deceive, a notice which could never have been intend to apprise the public of what was actually wanted by the company, was again issued and the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. A. H. Clarke) asked that the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders should deal with that question. We knew that we had to refer it to them. What ought we to do? We had practically a new Bill. Two provisions of that Bill had never been advertised before. One of them, the most important one, it was found had not been sufficiently advertised and so having come to this House it was necessary it should then go to the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders. Why should it not go to that committee according to the rule I have referred to? It was not sent to them in that way and until it was
sent to them in that way this House had not done its duty by the public.
That is all right.

I am glad to have for once concurrence of my hon. friend. On the motion of the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke), the order for the further consideration in Committee of the Whole of Bill (No. 56) respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company was discharged and referred back to the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders to inquire and report to this House what notice had been given the public and policy-holders. The order was not to inquire and report on the sufficiency of the notice, but to tell us what we could have found out by going to any newspaper, what we knew before that order was made, namely, what had been advertised in the press. There was the beginning of the second difficulty and that is where we are now. The Select Standing Committee might have done better, but we cannot complain of them because probably they might have done worse. In fact, they did nothing. They reported to us, in the terms of that order, that certain advertisements had been made, giving the dates and a copy of the notice. I called the attention of the right hon. gentleman who leads the House to the fact that on the 25th of March the committee reported that no sufficient advertisement had been made. The matter was then at an end, so far as the progress of this Bill is concerned. It had to begiu over again, if the Bill was to be dealt with. The Insurance Company then, of its own motion, began to advertise; and after they had done so this resolution was introduced, which does not comply with the rules of the House. The company did not present a new petition. They simply advertised, as they saw fit, and I can show to my right hon. friend that this second advertisement was no more honest than the first. Under these circumstances, there can be no doubt as to the duty of this House. Our duty is to send the Bill back to the Committee on Standing Orders and have that committee report to us regarding the sufficiency of the last notice issued.

It occurs to me that if the House proceeds with the motion now before the Chair and goes into committee on this subject, it will be defeating the very object for which notice of this kind of legislation is given. The first notice was passed upon and found insufficient. The company then went on to give further notice. What is the object of the rule requiring notice to be "Wen? It is that the parties interested should have an opportunity of being heard regarding the proposed legislation. There are two parties interested, the company and the policy holders. The companv has been heard. But we

are asked to move the House into commit-tee_ to consider the Bill without giving the policy-holders any opportunity of giving their opinion upon it. If we are to proceed with this measure without giving that opportunity, we shall be defeating the very object of the notice. In all justice and fairness, the Bill ought to be referred back t*>
the Committee on Standing Orders in order to give the policy-holders interested, or the provincial government on their bejhalf, an opportunity of discussing the provisions of the Bill. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has offered a fair and reasonable opportunity to accomplish that object, by asking that the Bill be referred back to the Committee on Standing Orders, in order that that committee may report whether sufficient notice has been given, and if the provincial government or the policy-holders should see fit to appear before the committee and represent their case, a special report might be made, although that report would not be binding on this House.

I venture to suggest that, although this Bill was referred back to the Committee on Standing Orders, to ascertain whether the notices were sufficient or not, that committee has not reported. The duty of that committee was to report whether or not that notice was sufficient. Under our new rules, the first procedure is to present a petition and have that taken into consideration by the examiner of petitions, whose duty it is to report to the House in each case the extent to which the requirements of the rules regarding notice have been complied with. It transpires that the House was not satisfied that the proper notice had been given and that the rules had been complied with. After the consideration of that by the House it was referred back to the Standing Orders Committee for further examination. Now if the examiner of petitions were not satisfied the rule says:
In every case where the notice is reported by the examiner to have been insufficient or otherwise defective, the petition shall be taken into consideration without special reference by the Committee on Standing Orders, who shall report to the House recommending the course to be taken in consequence of such insufficiency of notice or other defects therein.
Now did they do that? Did they recommend to the House what should be done in consequence of insufficiency of notice or other defects? They evidently did not. Then if they did not, the Standing Orders Committee did not do what the rule lays down that they should do, and therefore the House has a right to refer the Bill back to the same committee and ask them to report recommending the extent to which the requirements of the rules regarding notice have been complied with. Now it is quite clear, because they say so themselves, that
the notice was not sufficient, that a proper notice was not given, but they did not recommend to the House what the House should do in consequence thereof. Now in view of the fact that we have not such a report recommending the House what to do, nor have they reported clearly that the proper notices were not sufficient, or partially sufficient, then I say we have a right to refer it back to them, and get a proper report. Bourinot says that the House shall appoint a standing orders committee whose duty it shall be:
The said committee shall be empowered to examine and inquire into all such matters and things as may bew referred to them by the House.
All these petitions were referred to that committee by the House previously to the change in our rules. If that committee found these petitions defective in any way, the committee are to report from time to time their observations thereon. What observations? Whether the notice has been complied with or not? Did they give their opinion as to whether that rule had been complied with? Not at al . They gave us the report of their observations, and their observations were to the effect that the rule had not been complied with, because they referred to certain clauses of the Bill of which no notice whatever was given in the ' Gazette,' and they referred to other clauses where there was not a strict compliance with the rule. Therefore their observations and opinions thereon were not given fully to this House. It is therefore, in my opinion, the duty of the House to refer it back to that committee and ask them to make a proper report to the House as to their observations or findings, whether the rule requiring public notice to be given has been complied with in that second notice.

I understand it is necessary under rule 90, subsection C, that all such notices, whether inserted in the ' Canada Gazette ' or in a newspaper, shall be published at least once a week for a period of five consecutive weeks. But the five weeks was not allowed to elapse before the Bill was up before the Standing Orders Committee. I think this House should consider whether we are to allow Bills to go through in that way. I take it for granted that five weeks means that five full weeks must elapse before the Bill can be properly presented before the committee. The fifth week was only started, only one day had passed when the Bill was presented here. I think this Bill is a very important one. There are thousands and thousands of policy-holders throughout the Dominion to whom this notice was perhaps sent; but what time have they had to consider the importance of the Bill? One gentleman states that he never got a notice; at the

same time where a Bill like this is going to affect so many policy-holders and so many heirs that might receive benefits from this, I think the Canada Life Assurance Company should have given the policy-holders longer time, should have given them some months in which they might thoroughly understand what it meant; let them get together and give them an opportunity of stating their position before a committee of the House. The whole thing has been rushed through. If we allow this Bill to _ go through without the full five weeks notice, I think we will be establishing a very dangerous precedent. I cannot see where the Canada Life are going to lose anything by letting it stand over until another session. By that time every policy-holder in the Dominion will understand exactly the situation, and know that at the next session of the House the matter may come up again and be threshed out after ample notice has been given to the policy-holders. I think the government should allow it to stand over until the House meets in November, and then every policy-holder in Canada will have had ample notice. I do not understand exactly how this Bill affects the policy-holder, but I judge from the opposition that is being made to this Bill, that it is unfair to rush it through at this late date in the session. I hope the government will accept the motion of the hon. member for Halton, and let the Bill be withdrawn.
With regard to serving notices on every policy-holder. I may say that I am a policy-holder and I received no notice.

There are a number of gentlemen on both sides of the House who regard the additional notice as insufficient. But that question should not occupy the time of the House, that is particularly the function of the Standing Orders Committee to look into. Consequently I think that this motion is well put, and that the Bill should be referred back to the Committee on Standing Orders to consider the sufficiency or insufficiency of the notice. It is true, as the hon. member for South Essex says, that the committee reported all that the House ordered them to report, but the House did not order them to report enough. It was on the motion of the hon. member for South Essex that the specific reference was made to the Standing Orders Committee and that reference was not sufficient, because it did not ask the Standing Orders Committee to report upon the sufficiency or insufficiency of the notice. The time of the House should not be occupied with the consideration of the question of whether a notice is sufficient or not. We would have to examine the notice, we would have to examine the Mr. J. D. REID.
report of the committee brought down, and that might occupy some hours of the time of this House. I think the proper course to pursue is that which has been suggested by my hon. friend from Halton, that we send it back to the Standing Orders Committee to report upon. I venture to express the opinion that the promoter of the Bill would make more progress if he proceeds along the lines of least resistance, because, if he attempts to railroad this Bill through the House, he will find considerable opposition. This company has been the same as it is now for the past thirty years, and I do not see why there should be such undue haste in order to legislate the rights of 35,000 policy-holders away and transfer their profits into the pockets of the shareholders. I think the House should adopt the motion of my hon. friend from Halton and refer this Bill to the Standing Orders Committee for a proper report.
Amendment (Mr. Henderson) negatived.
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to move ano ther motion.
He is not leaving it.

If hon. gentlemen desire to facilitate the business of the House they should try to observe some rules of decorum. It is all right to have a few jokes but there is business to be done. It would be just as well if some hon. gentlemen would behave themselves. I only desire to say a few words in support of the motion which I am about to make. It is an important one, and I think it is even more im portant than the one which was moved by my hon. friend from Halton a moment ago I propose to move that:
Order No. 4 be discharged and that Bill (No. 56) an Act respecting the Canada Lifp Assurance Company, as amended by the Com mittee on Banking and Commerce, be refer red back to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce for further considera tion and report.
It will only be necessary to say a few words in support of this motion, although it is one that involves a good deal. A few weeks ago it was decided in this House that the advertisement had not been sufficient, that as regards the most important clause in the Bill no sufficient notice had been given and that, as regards two other clauses, no notice at all had been given. It is of the essence and fairness of a parliamentary contract, such as is now proposed, that every shareholder should have an opportunity of knowing exactly what the company propose and should have ample opportunity of presenting his views to the committee which has the matter in charge. That is the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce. We know that in this House there is no opportunity for any per

son to come and present his views, but that in the committee, now that certain notoriety has attached to this Bill, there will no doubt be a great number of people who will want to present their opposition to this pro posed legislation. Be that as it may, 1 need not elaborate the argument, which is this. There would be no object in further advertising this Bill, no object in giving notice to the public, unless we gave the public an opportunity to be heard. It would be the veriest farce to insist upon the most elaborate advertisement and then give no opportunity to interested policy-holders to present their views. It is said that this is the most perfect advertisement that possibly could be given, although I find three hon. gentlemen in this House within reach of my hand who say that they received no notice, notwithstanding the fact that they are policy-holders. It is said that the most elaborate advertisement has been published in this case, but it would be idle to have that advertisement given if there were no opportunity given the public of coming before a select standing committee and enunciating their views. Only one word more in reference to this. I think my right hon. friend the leader of the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will agree in the propriety of giving the policy-holders an opportunity of being heard. I think he will agree that now that the advertisement is said to have reached a great number of policy-holders, these policy-holders shall have an opportunity of coming before the Committee on Banking and Commerce and saying whether or not they think this- legislation ought to pass. They have never had any opportunity.
I am sorry, inasmuch as we have rather forced the views of the Ontario government upon the House to-day, that I have to refer again to the attitude of the Ontario government in this regard. Why should not the Ontario govenment be the special guardian of the interests of the people of Ontario? _ They surely have a mandate to act in that capacity. They have a sufficient majority at their back to make them astute in endeavouring to .safeguard the interests of the people whom they so abundantly represent. I will not read the whole of the order in council that has been referred to to-night, but I will Tead a clause or two that I specially wish to draw to the attention of the House. In the first part it is set out that it has been transmitted to the Dominion government. Therefore it is the less necessary that I should read the whole of it, but they say that:
The undersigned has had under consideration the Bill respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company now before the Dominion parliament, and respectfully recommends that a despatch be forwarded to the Secretary of State, Ottawa, regarding the Bill to the following effect:-
The Bill now before parliament regarding the Canada Life Assurance Company if it becomes law will in effect alter the contract of every policy-holder on the participation plan and largely reduce the amount that he is legally entitled to out of the profits under the existing law.
The extent to which such policy-holders will suffer if the Act is passed will be very greatly increased by the action of the directors and their shareholders in having unnecessarily increased the amount of the paid-up capital stock from $125,000 to $1,000,000 (see report of Eoyal Commission as to this). An opinion with regard to the law has been obtained by some policy-holders from Sir Robert Findlay.
They then proceed to set out in substance the opinion given, which I need not read to the House at this stage. The order continues as follows:
A large number of the policy-holders in the company reside in the province, and their property and civil rights which are within the jurisdiction of this province will be interfered with by such legislation as is proposed in the present instance.
Property and civil rights and provincial rights ! There is no more serious way in which we can invade the civil rights of a people than by saying that after a solemn contract has been entered into and has been sanctioned by parliament and has existed for thirty years, a few people may come before the House of Commons and before the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce and endeavour to put through a Bill which shall deprive these people of their rights and declare that which is known not to have been the law is the law.
Alter the contract?

Alter the contract.
The Bill having only recently passed the Standing Orders Committee, there is not sufficient time now that the session is approaching its close to fully consider the matter, and it is respectfully submitted that the government should procure the postponement of the consideration of the Bill until next session. The rights and the jurisdiction of the province are involved and. ample time should be given to the provinces of the Eom-inion to consider the matter and decide what course should be adopted by them.
That order in council was passed on the 30th April and said to have been forwarded to the Dominion government, so that I presume the government is in receipt of it. Well, if I am to assume from the Prime Minister that the government has not received it that only emphasizes the extreme haste with which this legislation is being promoted. I shall take the liberty of sending this order in council over to the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has appealed to me I must tell him I am very sorry I cannot

agree with any of his arguments. This Bill was referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee; it was examined by that committee and found satisfactory. When it came back to the House it was suggested by some members that the notice to the policy-holders had not been sufficient and that it was advisable to again refer the Bill to the Standing Orders Committee. I must say that it seemed to me that the original notices were amply satisfactory and quite sufficient for any intelligent man to ascertain what was the purpose of this Bill. However, some members of the House thought differently, and I did not interpose my own personal opinion to prevent the Bill being referred to the Standing Orders Committee. The last argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) is that the Ontario government has sent to us an order in council in which they say that this is a matter of provincial rights.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then I do not understand it.
They represent that this Bill affects a large portion of the people of Ontario; it is a matter of civil rights.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes; it concerns a certain number of the people of Ontario and also a certain number of the people of Quebec, and of Nove Scotia, and of New Brunswick, and of all the provinces, but I do not concede that the Ontario government has any right at all or any reason or any power to interfere in this matter. The Ontario government has the right to look after the business of the province of Ontario, which is confided to it by the British North America Act. I have been a friend of provincial rights in Ontario, and I had to defend them in my own humble way with the support of my friends around me, against the aggressions of hon. gentlemen opposite. In this matter the Ontario government has no standing at all, and it seems to me that the appeal made by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) cannot be entertained.

Let me ask the right hon. gentleman if it was anything more than a farce to have fresh notices given to the public if thje public were not to be allowed an opportunity to be heard on this Bill. If you advertise the sitting of a court you state where the court is to be held, in order that the parties may appear there, but in this case what was the use of advertising if the people affected were not to be given an opportunity to appear. The Prime Minister told us he did not consider it necessary to give new notices, but he was an assenting party to that procedure and being an assenting party he should now Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
give the people an opportunity to be heard. The only place they can be heard is before the committee or at the bar of the House, and nobody suggests that. As to the standing of the provincial government in thi3 matter, I apprehend that in the other provinces, as in Ontario, tne provincial governments _ are the guardians of the infants in each province. The rights and claims of the widows and orphans against the Canada Life Assurance Company are naturally in the guardianship of the provincial governments, and in that aspect the provincial government has something to say as to the amount of insurance that should be recovered on the death of the bread winner of a family. What possible excuse can there be for saying that an opportunity should not be given to some one to represent before a committee of the House that large class of people who are interested in this matter. Notice was given for five weeks to the world at large, and the province of Ontario is a large part of the world at large, and the government of Ontario have taken action. Unless this Bill is referred back to committee, the whole procedure of ordering new notices to be given is ridiculous. I cordially support the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox).

I am opposed to this Bill and to tne principle of the Bill, and I am specially opposed to its being forced on the House at the present time when the policy-holders-the men who are most interested in the Bill-have not had an opportunity of coming before this House and presenting their views. The Bill was referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, where it was dealt with to a certain extent; it came back to the House and it was found that no notice had been given, that any shareholder could become cognizant of, that it was proposed by the Canada Life Assurance Company to ask for legislation that would be retroactive and that would impair every contract that had been made with the 40,000 policyholders during the last thirty years. It was decided that the Bill had not been properly advertised. It was sent back to the committee, and, as the last speaker has pointed out, it has been re-advertised; and if this Bill is not to be referred back to the Banking and Commerce Committee, why was it advertised? Simply as a farce to deceive the policy-holders? Is this government going to be responsible for that sort of thing-to advertise a Bill, and not give the men interested in it an opportunity to come before a committee of this House and lay their case before it? To my mind it is a most peculiar proceeding. What is the great haste to push this Bill through the House? It has been on the statute book for the last thirty years and

the Canada Life has been doing business under it for that length of time. Will it hurt the Canada Life to wait six months more? In the ordinary course this House will be called together again in six months from now. We are in the dying days' of the session. Why not let the Bill stand over till next session, and then give the policy-holders an opportunity to get together and organize and come before the Banking and Commerce Committee and present their views? If they are given that opportunity, and cannot put up a good case, I for one will not have any further opposition to offer to the Bill. But. Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the Bill is bad in itself. There are contracts that have been made by this company during the past thirty years. Is there one word in either the first or second advertisement that would give the ordinary policy-holder to understand that this legislation proposed to be retroactive and took away the rights he was supposed to have had during all those years? I have the word of the president of the company that there are about 40,000 policy-holders, and there are hundreds and thousands of these who believe that they are being robbed, that their profits are being switched from them and taken by the shareholders. I am not going to say that that view is correct. I am not going to say that the views I hold, and they are pretty strong views, are correct. But I am going to say that when there are thousands of men who. believe that they have a grievance against the company, and this government comes in and says to those men that they shall not be allowed to come before a committee of this House and state their grievance, every one of those men will always bear in his mind the impression that he had a grievance. I have here a couple of policies of my own, and I believe the profits have been taken from those policies which should have come to them; and if this government passes this legislation this session without giving me and other policyholders an opportunity to come before the Banking and Commerce Committee and place our views before it, there is no power on earth that will make me believe in the future that I have not been robbed. And I do not stand alone in this matter. During the last month, since my name has been to a certain extent connected with the opposition to this Bill, dozens of policy-holders of this company in this city have come to me and have presented their views. I do not say that all the policyholders share these views. There may be many who are perfectly satisfied; but outside of the members of this House, I have not heard one man who is a policy-holder express himself as satisfied with the conditions-why? Because during the past
fifteen years, since this company has come under the present management, the profits of the policy-holders have simply dwindled down year after year; and these policy-holders would like to have some proper explanation of why a policy which twenty or twenty-five or thirty or forty years ago would earn $25 of profits in a year can now earn only $10. That is something the company ought to explain. That is something that if not explained will always stick in the minds of the policy-holders; and if the government does not give the policy-holders an opportunity to present their side of the case, the government will come in for a great deal of very adverse criticism. Why should this company be given all the consideration and the policy-holders none? Is there any good reason why the 40,000 policy-holders should have no consideration at all at the hands of this government or this parliament and this company get all the consideration? Just let me contrast two eases. A few years ago we had a Royal Commission on insurance, which made a report and submitted a draft Bill. The government, some three sessions or two sessions ago, introduced that Bill into the House. What would you have thought if an attempt had been made to rush that Bill through the House without giving the insurance companies an opportunity to come before the Banking and Commerce Committee and present their side of the case? Are the 40,000 policy-holders of this company entitled to less consideration at the hands of the government than this company and other insurance companies? I hope that that will never be said. What consideration has been shown to these insurance companies? In compliance with their request, this insurance Bill has been put off from year to year. It has been before the Banking and Commerce Committee for weeks and months; we have spent the last two sessions working at it, and the company now under discussion has during this session had four men here for weeks and months working to get that Bill into proper shape. I quite agree that they are perfectly right, and I will be just as ready to oppose any idea of passing a measure by shutting them out as I am opposed to shutting out the policy-holders on this occasion. There is the treatment that has been accorded to the companies and why should less good treatment be accorded to the policy-holders? I think they are entitled to some consideration If this legislation is passed this session without giving the policy-holders an _ opportunity to appear before the committee and represent their views, then so far as I am concerned politically, it will put me out of business. I have the honour or misfortune, whichever you like to call it, of



representing a constituency that has a Conservative majority and I have no hopes in the future of helping it out by redistribution simply because I am bounded on one side by the United States and on the other by the province of Manitoba and with the increase of population all I can do is to have the Liberal end of my constituency cut off. I was offered another constituency but I preferred to take the hard end and take the hard fight and I did it. If this resolution is passed and hundreds of my supporters on both sides are done out of their right to come before this House and before the Banking and Commerce Committee and present their views, even if they are wrong, every one of these men will have a grievance against the government and will vote against me. That puts me out of business. That of course is a very small matter and I do not mention it as of any great importance but I wish to tell my hon. friends on this side of the House there are a good many others in the same position.
Not many.

When the hon. member gets through I shall try to go on. There are a good many members in exactly the same position. A matter of a hundred votes makes a great difference and it is well to consider that phase of the question. We are piling up a grievance now that these men will remember, and I can assure you from what I have heard in the past month that this matter sinks far deeper into the minds of policy-holders of the Canada life than you have any idea of. I have men, men who did not wish their names mentioned, and you would be surprised at some of them, who have told me that they look on this Bill as a most iniquitous piece of legislation. One man told me that if this legislation passed he would want to sell his policy for what he could get for it, because he could have no confidence that this company would not come farward in ten years time asking for legislation and getting it that would deprive him perhaps of more than they are taking from him at this time. I think that is an extreme view and do not take that view, but it is held and I repeat that if you do not give these men an opportunity to present their claims they will have a just grievance and nothing will remove from their minds the feeling that they have been improperly dealt with. There can be only two reasons for pushing this through. One is that if it is not pushed through now it will be more difficult to get it through next session.
Perhaps this is the dividend year.
If that is the case it is a very good reason for delaying it. If the

Bill is as good as the Canada Life people say it is, what is their objection to having it go before the Banking and Commerce Committee, and allowing the policy-holders to present their views. If their contention is right and fair and just, the Bill will go through, and there will be no difficulty, but if the Bill is such that a thorough investigation into it and a thorough presentation of the case of the policy-holders would prevent it going through, is the government justified in pushing it through in the dying days of this session, without giving the policy-holders a single opportunity to come before the committee and present their views? That is the strong ground I take, not on the merits of the Bill. I have no uncertain feeling on the merits of the Bill but it is not on that ground that I am opposing its passage. These policy-holders, 40,000 of them, are depending on these policies for their wives and their children when they have passed over the great divide. There will be 40,000 widows probably one day depending on these policies, and there will be over 100,000 orphans-
All on one day?
Order.

-Depending on these policies. Surely in a matter of such importance it is not asking too much-and I appeal to the fairness and the good sense ut my honoured leader that it is surely not asking too much to request that this particular Bill stand over until next session and that the policy-holders should be given an opportunity to come before the committee and present their views of the case. I have heard it said: If this Bill is not passed this session, why there will be litigation! The only logical conclusion you can come to from this is that if this company has been doing wrong, has been going contrary to the law for thirty years, then you should pass legislation to make their course right for the past thirty years, give them the right to do wrong for all time to come and prevent for ever anybody taking action to obtain redress of their wrongs. The Minister of Justice the other day dealt very fully with this question and either he or some other member stated, while we were discussing the Cobalt Mining Company's deal, that the government of Ontario had no right to step in and pass legislation to do away with litigation between two parties, and I heard the statement-I will not say by the Minister of Justice-that the provincial government had no more right.to pass legislation that would prevent any man who felt aggrieved from going into litigation than to interfere in a case that had already been started. In this ease litigation has already been started so if we apply the rule laid down by the Minister of

Justice the government has no right to step in and prevent that litigation. If they have no right what right has this government or any government on earth to stand between me and the men who I believe have done me an injustice? I believe they have done me an injustice. Give me an opportunity next fall with other shareholders to place my views before the Banking and Commerce Committee and if I can be shown that no injustice is being done, that this is right, then I shall have nothing more to say. This is not the first time I have been up against this company in trying to get some information. For the last seven or eight years I have been trying to get some satisfactory answer to the question why the dividends on my policies have been cut down to almost nothing. I have never been able to get any satisfactory explanation. I could get a lot of smooth talk by insurance men who knew all about the subject while I did not know very much about it, but I never could get any reason that appealed to my sense of justice. I may be altogether wrong, but I want them to explain to me and their policy-holders how it is these profits have been so small. A great many of the policy-holders have made this complaint to me. Take the president of this company alone-and he is the president of half a dozen other companies and on the directorate of as many more- he draws a salary of $20,000 a year.
What has that to do with this Bill?

I propose to discuss this Bill in my own way. That $20,000 comes out of the pockets of_the policy-holders, who otherwise would get the benefit. That is what it has to do with this Bill. And the president has two sons in this company, one of whom draws $15,000 a year and the other $20,000,' making $50,000 per year to one family. That is what many of the policy-holders object to. What would this country think of the Prime Minister, if he voted himself $20,000 a year and then gave his two nearest relatives $15,000 and $20,000 respectively, and our Prime Minister devotes all his time to the work .and works hard. What would this side of the House say, if the leader of the opposition should come into power and immediately vote himself $20,000 a year and his two nearest relatives $15,000 and $20,000 per year? Would we not make the House resound with our denunciations? Why we would raise the roof off it and make every platform ring from the Atlantic to the Pacific. And remember there are over a million voters to pay those salaries, and those men to whom they would pay them give all their time to the work, whereas there are only 35 or 40 thousand policyholders paying these other men who do not give up all their time to their particular 1721
offices. That is one reason given by policyholders why their profits have been so small during the past fifteen years. There is a general feeling among the policyholders of the Canada Life that things have been manipulated in a very nice, smooth way, but in such a manner that the profits that should go to the policyholders do not go to them. That is the feeling abroad and that feeling will not down until those policy-holders are given the opportunity to organize and put their case before a committee of this House; and that they cannot do this session. They could not even do it properly if this Bill were referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee. There would be a small opportunity then to do something, but it would only be a makeshift. What I ask is that this legislation be allowed to stand over. If the Bill be a good one, as the hon. member for Essex (Mr. Clarke) says it is and as the government claim, there will be no trouble in putting it through then; but if it be forced through now there will be a great deal of dissatisfaction, as many of us will have Teason to know before the next general elections. A good deal has been said about the increase of capital. In 1900, the capital was increased from $125,000 to $1,000,000. At that time there was no need of more capital. The company had millions to its credit, it has millions invested, and remember that all that money is the money of the policy-holders, and only 10 per cent of the profits really belongs to the company. There were millions to the credit of the company, and the shareholders had their $125,000 paid up and were drawing 30 per cent to 70 per cent per annum on it. Was that not good enough? Should they not have been satisfied with that? And remember that the men who are drawing these big salaries own over 50 per cent, of the stock. Surely they ought to have been satisfied, but no, they increased their capital. They claimed that it was necessary, not so much on account of the money, but to have a better standing in the old country and the United States. Possibly there was something in that claim, but at all events they paid in this extra money, and a good many policy-holders believe that was done to benefit the shareholders at the expense of the policy-holders. I am inclined to that belief myself, but I am not sure that I am right. If the case were put before the committee and explanations made, I might be easily convinced that in that respect I am altogether wrong. I feel strongly on this question because I have a large number of policy-holders in my constituent, and it is not individually or personally that I ask my right hon. leader to put this measure off until next fall, but on behalf of the 40,000 people I represent in this House. It is in their interest I ask that this legislation be delayed until next ses-

sion. Remember this is a matter of vital importance to thousands of people in this country-men on salaries who have paid in all their savings of a life time, whose savings are locked up in policies in this company. They are the men who feel aggrieved and who want to be represented. Why treat the corporations with one kind of justice and the policy-holders with another? Why not give even-handed justice to both? This is just a little trouble between the policy-holders and the company, why should not the government leave us alone to settle our own difficulties without interfering? We will settle them and there will be very little trouble about it. All we want is a good explanation. I want to make that point as clear as possible. I am not discussing the Bill on its merits at all, but I am insisting on the right of the policy-holders -the men who have put up the $33,000,000 invested by the company-to be given a hearing before the committee. I leave it to the fairness of the Prime Minister to say whether or not this legislation should stand over for six months. The company have worked for 30 years under their present incorporation, why not let them work under it six months longer? I ask the right hon. the Prime Minister to consider thi3 carefully and see whether he cannot let this legislation stand until six months, and I venture to say it will go through then with one-tenth part of the difficulty it will take to put it through now.

I have a few observations to make on this motion, and in so doing I purpose to keep religiously away from discussing the Bill on its merits. If the_ House will do me the credit of believing that I can for a moment discuss a question entirely apart from partisan consideration, I assure them that is my intention. If I understand the right hon. the Prime Minister correctly, and that he is determined to force this Bill on the consideration of this House, aside from the Banking and Commerce Committee, that is a course the most utterly inexplicable on the part of the government since I have been a member. Some few weeks ago when this Bill was before us and was referred back to the Standing Orders Committee, and when they reported the Bill had not been sufficiently advertised, who would have understood when a further advertisement was ordered by this House, that that advertisement had no purpose at all? There might have been some difference of opinion as to the last motion, it might have been of a technical oharacter; but, surely, on this motion that, after this Bill had been advertised for the purpose of making its contents known to the public, surely on this motion that proposes to give them a chance to be heard, there should be no difference of opinion. No. hon. gentleman Mr. TURRIFF.
has ever attempted to answer the query as to what object there could have been in advertising this measure to the country if the country is not to be heard. The Prime Minister avoided that point in his speech. Now where does the government stand? The government of Ontario come before this House, and they present a protest against this Bill. I do not conceive the government of Ontario in doing so made any claim to this House by passing the legislation embodied in Bill 56 invaded at all provincial jurisdiction, but really acted on the principle of the government of Ontario is in a sense the custodian of the civil rights of the citizens of Ontario, and as such custodian it protests against this Bill, which they claim is an invasion of those civil rights. Now the Prime Minister says, we will not go before the Banking and Commerce Committee, we will not let the policy-holders be heard there. If that is the decision of this government, then by * what method could the government of Ontario ever be heard before this House, except by the very method they have adopted? If we are to shut out all representatives before the Banking and Commerce Committee, which I understood was the medium by which the public could be heard before parliament, then the method adopted by the government of Ontario is the only method any government or any individual could adopt to make its or his opinions known in this* House. Therefore the government are in this position: If a provincial government comes to us by petition asking that this legislation be not passed, we resent it and we also deny to the people represented by that government the right to come before us in any other way. Surely that is tyranny personified. I say the action of the government in this respect is inexplicable to me, and I hope some good reason will be given for it before this matter is disposed of.

I am glad to have heard the argument of my learned friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and also of the other hon. gentlemen who are so strongly opposed to the Bill before the House. A good many speak of it as being inexplicable. From my understanding of the question, it is inexplicable to me that a Bill designed to do a simple and ordinary act of justice, as this Bill is designed to do, should be resisted in the vicious manner in which this Bill is being resisted by certain pnities.
I did not say the Bill v>:i.i inexplicable, I said the action of the government was inexplicable.

I was not referring to my hon. friend. I was saying that it

appeared inexplicable to me that where people do understand the Bill, they are putting up such a strenuous opposition. I have not heard, even in the heated argument of the hon. member for Assinihoia, one cogent reason against the passing of this Bill. He has made many strong statements about what the policy-holders say; I have heard just as strong statements from the policy-holders saying the government would not do its duty, saying it would be a great loss to and undoing of the policyholders, if the present Bill were not passed, and giving strong reasons why it should pass at this session. Now what is this Bill for? The object of the Bill is a simple one. The Canada Life Company come to this parliament, which created the company, the only legislature, the only tribunal which can deal with the matter, and say that in the legislation which was passed in 1879 at the instance of the company, words were used which, in the opinion of an eminent counsel in England, it is said, do not bear the interpretation which it was intended they should bear by the company who promoted it. Now if there was a mistake, if the interpretation of Sir Robert Findlay is correct, I entertain not the slightest doubt, I am positively convinced, that the interpretation which is sought to be put upon the Act of 1879 is absolutely foreign to the intention of any person present at the time, foreign to the understanding of the directors and of the policyholders from that time to the present.
Would not the courts so decide, and then what is the need of your Bill?

I will come to that point presently. I was saying that I am convinced that there is a mistake, and that to pass this Bill is to do an act of simple justice. If the legislation were not a statute, if it were a contract, the terms thereof could be reformed by the court, because in that case the court would have jurisdiction to reform. I am satisfied also, not only that it is an act of common justice to the shareholders, but it is an act of the greatest importance to the policy-holders of this company.
If that is so, why not let the Banking and Commerce Committee hear the policy-holders say that for themselves?

Will my hon. friend wait till I make my argument? I am satisfied that, however much this Act is in the interest of the shareholders of the Canada Life Company much more is it in the interest of the policy-holders; because if there is some temporary disarrangement in the dividends paid to the shareholders, that is a matter in which the shareholders can protect themselves and recoup themselves. But if the
directors or shareholders refuse to exercise the rights which they have and decline to declare profits in the future, or if, having cut down the dividends, an incentive to make a successful company does not exist, then it is the policy-holders in respect of their profits that must suffer, because the amount of profits they receive is intimately bound up in the success of this company. Now, let us look at the history of the company in Canada.
I rise to a point of order. Is it pertinent to the question before the Chair for the hon. gentleman to give a history of the company?

The motion before the Chair is to refer this Bill to the Select Committee on Bankine and Commerce. The hon. member is giving reasons, I presume, why that should or should not be done. I do not think a detailed discussion of the Bill would be in order at this stage.

It was my intention to adduce arguments why this Bill should be proceeded with at once. If I go too wide of the mark, of course I will be called to order. I did not hear my hon. friends, who were so enthusiastic when my hon. friend from Assiniboia spoke, call him to order.
He did not discuss the merits of the Bill.

When he was talking about the high salaries being paid, or about the paid-up capital stock, had that nothing to do with the Bill? There was no objection whatever at that time, and I am a little surprised that my hon. friend should be so partial to my hon. friend from Assiniboia that he will not listen to me with as much grace as he listened to him. I will not trouble the House very long. I think it is well, however, that we should have a thorough understanding of this Bill, because the opinion which has been expressed by a great many people is something so foreign to my understanding of the Bill that I cannot understand the opposition which is being offered to it. In 1847 this company was incorporated by a deed of settlement. In that deed of settlement there was a provision with respect to profits. It provided that for the first two years no profits should be paid to the policy-holders, but thereafter the directors were empowered-they were not compelled but empowered-to declare profits from the participating business only and the profits were to be declared in the proportion of 75 per cent to policyholders and 25 per cent to the shareholders. In 1849 the first Act was passed. The company came to this parliament and got an Act of incorporation. When you speak about vested rights, if there has ever been any case of interference with vested rights in connection with this company, it was in 1849, because, prior to that time upon a

division of profits, the policy-holders were entitled to 75 per cent, but by the Act of 1849, that limitation was removed and the directors were empowered to allot such a proportion of profits as, in their judgment, they saw best.

The hon gentleman has surely disclosed quite clearly the line that he is pursuing. If anything can be manifest it is that he is discussing the merits of the Bill on the motion that this matter be referred back to the Banking and Commerce Committee. This motion does not in any sense involve the question of the merits of the Bill pro or con. I submit that the hon. gentleman cannot delay the passage of the Bill or the adoption of the motion in this way. It is simply a matter of obstruction. Although I do not want to interfere unduly with the hon. gentleman I think he should be called to order. I ask for the Tuling of the Chair.

The question before us is very plain. It is a motion to refer the Bill to the Banking and Commerce Committee. I am not the judge of the reasons that any hon. gentleman may give for or against this measure being adopted, but if the hon. gentleman proposes to discuss the details of the Bill upon this motion it is certainly out of order. The main motion is that the House go into committee on a number of Bills this one included.

Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that if there is a motion for the House to go into committee on a Bill you may discuss the merits of the Bill, and if some body else moves in amendment that the Bill should be referred to some committee it would not preclude the discussion of the general principle of the Bill.

The difficulty is that the main motion asks me to leave the Chair so that the House may go into committee on a number of Bills not only upon this one. Of course, if the contention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is correct, all the other Bills could be discussed in the same way. The main motion is merely pro forma, because, under the new rules, it is generally adopted without discussion so that the House may immediately go into committee on these Bills. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. H. Clarke) had better limit himself to the motion before the Chair.

Of course, I cannot make my argument complete unless I go into the merits of the Bill, because I want to lay the foundation for the argument I intend to close up with ; that is that so great a delay would be most dangerous to the interest of the policy-holders. I cannot do that properly unless I give the House my views on the merits of the Billl
generally. Now, I was pointing out

I am coming to that just as soon as I can and in logical order. I was saying, in giving a history of the legislation in regard to this company, that in the Act of 1849 there was no limitation whatever of the proportion of profits to be divided amongst the policy-holders and shareholders. The parliamentarians of that day did not think they were interfering very seriously with vested rights because prior to that Act the policy-holders were absolutely entitled to 75 per cent of the profits, which right was entirely taken away by the Act of 1849. After the Act of 1849 they could be allotted one per cent, or two per cent, or no per cent at all, if the company were so advised. So that we have the strongest precedent for the measure which is being brought in dealing with a distribution of profits between them. Notwithstanding the Act of 1849 the practice of the insurance company was to divide the profits in the proportion of 75 per cent to 25 per cent. This was continued down to 1879 when the Bill which is causing the present difficulty was brought before the House. What was the reason for bringing that Bill before the House? Mr. Speaker, I rise again to a point of order. I am going to endeavour to see if we are to have any rules of procedure at all. The hon. gentleman, for ten minutes more, has gone on with the history of the legislation of this company. This has no reference whatever to the motion before the Chair. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to rule, and to insist upon your ruling being observed.

The question before the Chair is simply whether this Bill should be referred to the Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce. The main motion asks the House to go into committee on a number of Bills on the Order Paper.

I would like to suggest that the House ought to be in possession of the facts that would enable hon. members to arrive at a conclusion whether or not we should go into committee on the Bill. The negative of the motion of the

hon. member for Simcoe is quite as pertinent as the positive side of that motion. Those of us who want to know what are the facts in connection with this matter ought, on this motion, or on the motion of which my hon. friend has moved in amendment, to have ample opportunity to know what the merits of this Bill are and which motion should be adopted. It is perhaps germane to this question of order to point out that my hon. friend who quoted from a minute of the Attorney General of Ontario as to the interest of the policyholders might perhaps consider the question as to the right of policy-holders who are members of this House to vote upon or discuss perhaps a measure in which they are personally interested.

The matter is simply this: It has been brought to the attention of the House that certain advertisements were issued, and if these advertisements are to be effective the matter should be referred now to the Banking and Commerce Committee to reconsider the question of whether this Bill should be passed or not ot whether we should hear the parties who may come before the committee so that they can report the matter back to the House.
