Bourinot says:
It has been frequently decided in the English House that on a motion for the Speaker to leave the chair a member is at liberty to discuss the main provisions but not to proceed in detail through the clauses in order to discuss amendments to the same, until the Bill is regularly in committee.
That is what I have held.

That is precisely what I understood and what I was intending to do. My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) does not seem to like to hear me, but I have listened to a great many speeches from him to-day and I think he might return me the compliment for this one speech. In 1879 an Act was passed which the present Bill is intended to rectify.
Chair.
The hon. member (Mr. Clarke) is an old member of the House; he understands what the ruling is and I am quite sure he will abide by it.

The whole difficulty has been caused by the anxiety of the framers of the Bill of 1879 to include the profits of non-participating policies as well
as of participating policies, and they use the words which, according to the opinion of Sir Robert Findlay, go beyond the intention and practice of every other insurance company doing business in Canada.
What words do you refer to?

'All the profits.' Up to 1879 the directors were not authorized directly by the statute then in force to divide among policy-holders the profits arising from anything but participating policies. That is to say, profits arising from annuities or from the non-participating branch. The directors were not authorized by the Act of 1849 to distribute amongst the participating policy-holders. That being so it was competent for any stockholder to find fault with the action of the directors for exceeding their authority. if the stockholders were not unanimous any one of them would have the right to say to the directors: You have no right to distribute these profits on nonparticipating policies amongst the participating policy-holders, but they should be paid in dividends to the stockholders. One of the objects of the Act of 1879 was to give authority to the directors ito do what they had in practice been doing, although they were not expressly authorized to do it. In the preamble they use the words which are the vital point in this discussion. That preamble says:
Whereas, the Canada Life Assurance Company have by their petition represented that in carrying on their business heretofore the directors have allotted and divided among all persons assured upon the participation scale 75 per cent of all the profits.
That is the important part of it.
Realized from the entire business of the company.
It says 'all the profits from the enitire business.' That means from every source.
The recital says they have been doing that.
That is an allegation of fact, and upon that allegation policies were taken ,out.
The allegation is thaJt they have been dividing heretofore all the profits of the insurance business.
From the .entire business; not from the insurance business That includes the capital as well as the iD surance.

I will read it again:
All the profits realized from the entire business of the company.

_ The statement of fact in that Act of 1879 is that theretofore they had been dividing all the .profits from the entire business of the company. If up to that time they had been dividing the profits derived from the investment of the capital stock then they would have no right to come here and say there is any mistake. But what they say is that that was not intended to mean what it is now said to mean, namely, that the interest on the capital stock should be treated as part of the profits of the business. The evidence is abundant and cannot be controverted, because every person who knows anything about it says that such was not the practice before 1879. Mr. Ramsay, who was president of the company at the time and who was president almost all his life; the actuaries who looked into it; Mr. Bruce who was the solicitor for many years
Were these gentlemen called before the Banking and Commerce Committee to .give their evidence?
Mr. Bruce was there.
Did he make a statement before the committee?
I am not a member of the committee and do not know, but I have the certificate of Mr. Ramsay which was distributed to the policy-holders.
That is not a statutory declaration.

Well, you can accept Mr. Ramsay's word just as well as you could a statutory declaration. Very well then, you have the statement of all these people that never in the whole history of this company have they distributed amongst the policy-holders any part of the interest on the capital stock, so that, if in the recital of the Act of 1879 you construe the words ' all the profits ' as meaning the interest on the capital stock, then certainly the allegation is a mistake, because they never have been doing that at all. I find fault with the statement of the case which was submitted by Mr. Laidlaw, of Toronto, who has been very active in opposition to this Bill, to Sir Robert Findlay. Mr. Laid-law says:
It is, therefore, not necessary for the purposes pf the opinion to refer to any payment of dividends or allotment of profits before the passing of the Act of 1879. The company is bound by the recital in the preamble to the Act of 1879, and clause one of the Act, inclusive, of the said proviso.
That is the kernel of the whole matter.
I would judge that in submitting to counsel a statement of facts it was of the utmost importance to have pointed out to Sir Robert Findlay that up to 1879, what the Act of Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
1879 calls ' all the profits ' did not include the profits arising from the investment of the capital stock.

Whatever may have been the practice before the Act of 1879, when this Act was passed with that preamble in it, would not the parties who took out policies after that date be correct in understanding that the division of the profits was to be on the entire business, and that that entire business included the earnings on capital as well as the earnings on policies?
If he did not know what the practice of the company was, I think it might be open to that construction.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friends say ' hear, hear,' but if it were not for that fact we would not be here to-night. If it were not for the opinion given by Sir Robert Findlay we would not be here with this Bill; it was because of that opinion the doubt was raised. He has said, upon the statement Tendered to him, that the meaning of the Act is not what every one intended it should mean, and so the company has come here to make the meaning plain.
Did my hon. friend hear the member for Hamilton state in committee that there was no doubt at all but that in a court of justice the opinion of Sir Robert Findlay would be sustained?

If the opinion ol Sir Robert Findlay is. sustained, that is the best answer I can give for coming here before the high court of parliament. Hon gentlemen shake their heads, but I can refer to much higher legal authority than I am. If they look at the case of Richards vs. McBride, in England, they will find it decided that if the draftsman has made a mistake, it is for the legislature to rectify it.
That mistake would have to be mutual; that is to say it must not deceive the policy-holders. Vou must not say that because you have made .a mistake, the policy-holders must suffer for it.

I will come to that. The question I am discussing is, is this the proper tribunal to rectify a mistake? The difficulty here is that the courts have such a high opinion of parliament that they treat it as not making any mistakes. It is pointed out in one case that the legislators are ideal persons who never make a mistake, and we do not want to undeceive them on that point.
Would not we make u mistake if we took away the rights of the policy-holders on the representations of other people?

That is a question of opinion which each member of the House must decide for himself. Unless I have heard more than I have heard yet, I am of opinion that we would be doing a decided injury to the policy-holders if we did not pass this Bill. I have pointed out that the Act of 1879 has been asked for by the company. If there was anything in the history of that Act to show that the capital stock was to be invested for the benefit of the policy-holders, it was never suggested in the House. The Bill was introduced by Mr. Robertson, of Hamilton, in a very simple statement, which you will find in 'Hansard' of 1879:
Mr. ROBERTSON (Hamilton) explained that, according to the original Act of incorporation, the company had power to divide its profits between the participating policyholders and the shareholders in the proportion of three-fourths to the policy-holders and one-fourth to the shareholders. This Bill proposed to extend this proportion to not less than ninety per cent to the participating policy-holders, and not to exceed ten per cent to shareholders. The only persons who could possibly object to this would be the stockholders, and they, at a general meeting called for the purpose, resolved to carry out the suggestion of the directors.
He did not suggest for a moment that the character of the profits that had been divided theretofore was to be altered, but simply that the proportion of the profits were to be altered. I have pointed out that those profits did not include the investments in the capital stock, and I have not heard in all the discussion on this Bill any person say that it would be just to the Canada Life Company to impose upon it the interpretation which it is said the Act of 1879 ought to bear.
We have not come to that yet.	.

We have come to it in other Bills in this very session, which required the companies to do only what the Canada Life has done. The legislation put through this session requires the companies to divide amongst the participating policy-holders only the profits arising from the participating branch.
They have not made any contract to the contrary.

That has nothing to do with it. I venture to say that there is no company in Canada and no British company doing business in Canada that does what the Canada life has been doing during the last thirty years with respect to its profits. You will look through the Acts of incorporation of the different companies in vain to find one which provides that the company shall divide amongst the policyholders both the participating and the nonparticipating profits. If you look over the report of the Royal Commission on Insurance, you will find that in every instance the companies have done precisely what the Canada Life has done, that is: First divide the interest on the capital stock among the shareholders before they make the division among the policy-holders. The Canada Life has gone further than other companies in this respect. Let us look at the Sun Life and see what it has done.

Does not the hon. member think this discussion would be better, in committee? Yes.

That is the way the rule is drafted.

Before the amendment is negatived?
Mr. BRODFT'^ Certainly.

Which includes the Hudson Bay Railway, the Algoma Central Railway and the Canada Central Bill. Does not the hon. gentleman see the absurdity of this?

I merely wish to ascertain just what His Honour, Mr. Speaker, has Tuled. Do I understand, Sir, that you have ruled that on a motion to send this Bill to a committee it is impossible to discuss the alternative of the propositipn, namely, that this Bill should go to the Committee of the Whole House?

I suppose he may discuss the main provisions of the Bill.

The reason I was going into the matter at considerable length was that my fellow members who had not studied the Bill carefully were anxious before voting on this motion to have a thorough understanding of the case. If I am precluded from explaining, of course, they will not have the benefit of the light I hope to shed around them and will have to vote without it. I will have to abandon a good deal of what I wish to say. My reason for opposing its being sent to the Banking and

Commerce Committee is the urgency of having it passed this session. This is the year when the profits will have to be apportioned to the policy-holders if there are to be any profits this year. The custom of the company has been to divide these profits every five years. In 1904 the profits which had been earned in the five preceding years were divided amongst the policy-holders, some having them added to their policy, some having them go in the reduction of the premium and some receiving the benefit in cash. The time for another division comes this year. As a policy-holder, T have a verv strong objection to putting this company in such a position that the profits on my policies will be cut off. The company has now got to a position when the profits ought to be very materially increased. Ten years ago they were very considerably decreased, because at that time they had to put up the main part of the reserve which was required by the government. Five years after that the profits were considerably increased, that is at the last quinquennial division. That reserve having been put up, it is reasonable to expect that this year there will be a considerable further increase in the profits. If we are to prevent the company from getting this legislation and they are left in a position of uncertainty, with the prospect of lawsuits. I think any sane directors will say: We will not declare any profits until we know what our position is. They are not bound to declare any profits, to be divided amongst policy-holders, they need not declare them from now until kingdom come. Many members have an entire misapprehension of what these profits mean. There is no law, by contract or statute, which requires the directors to give any profits to policy-holders.
What would the company under these circumstances do with the profits?

The company under these circumstances would accumulate the profits. The effect of this would I think be to ruin the company. If you are going to reduce the dividends from 8 per cent to less than 4 per cent, you will not find any directors enthusiastic about making the business profitable for the benefit of the policy-holders who put them in that position. It will be easy for them to say: we will quit business, let your policies expire, and settle with the policy-holders as their policies mature from time to time. This year, in the natural order- of things, they would divide profits, but as business men, they are certainly not going to take the risk of dividing profits with this claim hanging over their heads. The result, therefore, would be that every policy-holder would be up in arms because he was not getting any profits at all. Those who are now getting $10 on small policies would get nothing;
and those with large policies would suffer more still. You would then find that instead of the Canada Life asking for this Bill, the policy-holders would be swarming around us insisting that it should be passed. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr Turriff) talked of meeting these angry men. Well, I have met them-as good business men as you will find anywhere-in my own riding. They were not satisfied with everything. They thought that the directors paid up that reserve sooner than they needed, and that the salaries in some cases were too high, but that has nothing to do with the Bill. They realized that if the company were going to pay any profits, it must do a profitable business. But if you are going to cut the company down, so that it cannot do a profitable business, that may be a temporary inconvenience to the shareholders but the ultimate loss will come from the pockets of the policy-holders. Every argument that has been raised to-night, every argument that can be raised, was raised before the Banking and Commerce Committee, and it would not be complimentary to the policy-holders who were then heard, to say that others can present better arguments than they have been able to do.
With reeard to the power of the company, to withhold a division of the profits is it not a portion of their contract and included in each policy that the company will divide the profits periodically?
No, not a word of it, the company did not agree to anything of the sort. Let the hon. gentleman read his policy.
I have no policy in the company.
I have.
If that is not the case, is it not a fact that their agents represent to the people they try to induce to go into the company, that this was the invariable rule and would be done?

No. I have been canvassed ' by as many agents as most people, and I know the contrary. The statute does not bind the company nor does the policy. The policy-holders will accept such profits as are allotted to them. There is nothing that compels the company to allot profits to the extent of one cent. If they do allot profits, the proportions are fixed but they are not bound to.
What is the interpretation of the word ' may ?'

The directors are authorized by the shareholders. The stat-

ute says that the directors have the power to allot profits. Before 1879 they did not have that authority. This statute says: They may, and that shows the importance of proceeding at once. Surely everything that can be urged, has been urged, and it seems to me that the course we are asked to take would be absolutely the undoing of the policy-holders; and as a policy-holder myself I protest against people who claim to be our friends taking a course which is going to work mischief to our detriment. I submit that the Bill should not go back to the committee. It has been fully discussed and the Committee of the Whole is fully competent to deal with it.
I have a letter here from a policy-holder who has written me several times and who tells me he has entered suit to recover his rights under his contract.
What is his name?

His name is Chadwick and he is from Toronto. His letter is dated the 27th of March, and in it he says that the writ was issued a few days ago and was served on the company yesterday. He says further that other writs are to follow and he intends to prosecute his suit until it reaches the highest court in the Dominion. Surely, he says, the government are not going to confiscate what belongs to me under the contract.

I have the writ before me. It is against the Canada Life Assurance Company and asks the company to pay back all those dividends which have been paid the shareholders. How do you expect the company to be able to pay any profit to anybody if they have to pay the back dividends?

The question is whether we should interfere with the civil right of any one to prosecute a suit for the purpose of compelling a delinquent to carry out his contract. That is where the provincial government comes in. This is part of the civil rights of the people. The province is charged with the responsibility of looking after the rights of infants and orphans not able to look after their own. This is part of the civil rights, and my correspondent says: Am I to be denied the right of going	before the Banking and
Commerce	Committee and submitting
my case? I replied that the only way was for him either to appear before the bar of the House or before a committee of the House, which method parliament has devised as the most convenient. I replied further that I believed this Bill would be sent back to the Banking and Commerce Committee, after it was considered by the Standing Orders Committee, that is, if it should be taken up again this session, and that then every policy-holder Mr. A. H. CLARKE.
would have the opportunity of going before that committee and convincing parliament through it that his rights in that contract should not be taken away. But that now is denied, and the farce is to be perpetrated of having a notice published in the ' Gazette ' and then not allowing the interested parties to whom that notice was given to appear before the committee and vindicate their grievances.

The right hon. the Prime Minister in giving his reason for not allowing this Bill to go before the Banking and Commerce Committee, said that it had already gone before the Standing Orders Committee and that committee had said that the necessary advertising had been done. As a member of that committee,- I wish to say that the ground there taken was that the committee was not authorized to adjudicate whether sufficient notice had been given, but only to report w'hat notice had been published. One of the members of that committee cited cases to prove that the notices given were not sufficient, but the objection was taken and that objection prevailed that the committee was not empowered to consider that matter but only to report what notices had been given. I personally asked that a rider should be added to the report of the committee asking that the Bill be sent back Co the Banking and Commerce Committee in order that the policy-holders might be heard. There is no necessity for me to reiterate the argu-meftts which have been made to-night. There can be no doubt to my mind that it would be an absolute farce for this House as a Committee of the Whole to dispose of this Bill. The Bill was sent, as I have said, to the Standing Orders Committee. They reported the Bill back, not saying that the notice was sufficient, but merely saying what the notice was. The hkm. member for South Essex (Mr. Clarke) said that the company had readvertised the Bill. Then I ask what was the object of readvertising that Bill if it were not that the policyholders might be heard in regard to it. All we are asking here is that they may have the privilege and advantage of that readvertising, that all the parties may be heard. The hon. member for South Essex says that no argument has been advanced from this side of the House or by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) why this Bill should not be gone on with. Well, if they have not advanced any such argument, then I say it is impossible to understand any force in reason and logic. There Was one particular point raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia which I think is of vital importance. He intimated that there is a general feeling abroad that when the interest of the people comes into conflict with the interest of corporations, it

is the interest of the people that goes to the wall. If that is so, then I say that no more important question has been raised in this House since the session commenced. It is vitally important that the country at large should be satisfied that we are here as defenders of the public interest, and not of the interest of any corporation or individuals. I am not going to undertake to answer the arguments of the hon. member for South Essex, though I think they could be easily answered, but I want to keep within the ruling of the Speaker. I am now simply speaking to the question whether the amendment before the House should be adopted, or whether this Bill should be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee in order that the people may be heard. As a member of that standing committee I may say that they took the view they were not there to adjudicate on the merits of the Bill, but simply whether it should be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee, and on that ground we reported it. I would ask that every member in this House, realizing the claims of the great public, should give them another chance to be heard. There is no doubt a feeling of unrest throughout 'the country, which is shown by the rise of 'socialism and other fads based on the contention that justice is not being done to [DOT]the people in dealing with matters such as this. It is therefore of the utmost importance that we should give every opportunity to all the interests to be heard on this question, and on that ground I ask that this Bill be referred to the Committee on Banking and .Commerce in order that every man and woman interested in it may feel that parliament is looking after their [DOT]rights.

I would like to say a word in regard to the amendment that this Bill should be referred back to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce. I am opposed to that course, and for reasons which I believe are impartial. I have no interest in the matter, except that of a holder of a participating policy in the Canada Life Assurance Company. I was present during the discussion in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and I may say I think we had a very full and free discussion on the Bill without discussing whether it had been advertised as fully as it should have been or not. It was very fully and ably discussed by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson), and to some extent by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), and ably discussed by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and others. The" company had its representatives there. Most of those who took part in the discussion were policy-holders and interested parties, and I think I am within the mark when I say that every man who saw fit to attend the sittings of that committee when this Bill was under discussion had every opportunity to come to a conclusion. After an unprejudiced and impartial discussion, without any partisanship, without any political feeling, the hon. member for Halton, who undertook the chief part of the discussion, did not see fit to divide the committee upon the question. Then it came back to the House. On the 22nd of March it was fairly well discussed in this House, until somebody took the point that insufficient notice had been given, or that the notice given was not sufficiently explicit. Then the Bill went back to the Standing Orders. We know what the Standing Orders Committee reported, and what they were authorized to report. What I fear now is that if this amendment carries this Bill will not he advanced this session. I do not doubt the bona fides of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in his amendment, and certainly my hon. friend from Assiniboia has made it quite plain what his object is. He does not want the Bill advanced during the present session, but postponed until next fall. I take the ground as a policy-holder on the participating plan that that course will injure the policy-holders and injure the company, and that anything which is an injury to the company will be an injury to the policy-holders. It is idle to say that' the policy-holders as interested parties cannot be heard in response to the notice which has recent]v been .given. It is open to the policy-holders to be fully heard before the bar of this House, either in person or by counsel. All their grievances can be heard. It is open to them to be heard bv petition, and they can be heard through their representatives.
Why not in the usual way before the ordinary committee?

My only objection to that course is that a reference again to the Banking and Commerce Committee will involve delay and the defeat of this Bill for the present session. I am aware of the technicalities which are sometimes employed to delay a Bill. I do not, as I say, doubt the good faith of the hon. member who has moved this amendment, and the hon. member for Assiniboia has made his view quite plain. He says he and his friends want it put off until next fall. I think it would he disastrous to put it off. If the Bill goes to the Banking and Commerce Committee the discussion there may he interminable, and the Bill will not be advanced during the present session, if the present session is going to come to an end wdthin a reasonable time.
Who would suffer?

I think that probably chaos would follow. Actions would be brought against this company by the policy-holders, or by the company against the directors, and this would involve the credit of the company and would materially affect the profits. The policy-holders would suffer as a result of postponement. I believe it is in the interest of all parties that this Bill should be considered and considered now.
Does the hon. gentleman think it is the right and the duty of parliament to legislate men out of court?

No, I do not as a general rule think they should be legislated out of court, but I think it is the duty of this parliament, if a wrong has been done in the past by legislation, to put that wrong right at the earliest possible moment. I do not desire to discuss the merits of the Bill. I have examined it, I have considered it, and I have come to my own conclusion upon it. When the Bill comes up for discussion in the House I certainly intend to exercise my judgment in regard to it without expressing what that judgment shall be at the present time. But I think it is the duty of hon. members in the interest of the policy-holders and of the company to advance this measure and not retard it as they would by the adoption of the motion of the hon. member for South Simcoe.
Does the hon. gentleman realize that the course he advocates will prevent an investigation as to whether there is a wrong being done by this Bill or not?

No, I do not take that view of it. I think hon. members are quite capable of investigating that matter in this House. I think that forty or fifty per cent are policy-holders and interested parties and that they will take care of the interests of the policy-holders at large.

Following on the question asked the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), if the hon. gentleman believes as he does that it is not in the interest of the policy-holders to so embarrass the company by suits, does he think it is any part of the duty of this parliament to say to the policy-holders that it is not in their interest to sue the company or are not the policy-holders the best judges of that?
I think the House will be able to judge of that when the Bill is discussed.

I assume that the House is anxious to divide upon this question and I shall only say a few words. I have not heard one substantial argument for refusing the motion which is before the House now. It is claimed by the promo-Mr. LANCASTER.
ter of the Bill (Mr. A. H. Clarke) that a mistake was made in 1879. It was claimed by the hon. gentleman who spoke last that a wrong had been done. I want to draw the attention of the House to these statements. These matters came before the committee and I want to explain why I think it is a proper thing that the Bill should go 'back to the committee again. It is on account of the very discussion that we had in the Banking and Commerce Committee before. It was alleged in the Banking and Commerce Committee that a mistake had been made. So strong was the assurance that many of us in the committee really thought that some mistake had been made. A letter was even produced from Mr. A. G. Ramsay, who had been manager of the company for a long time, and who had been a director on the board. That letter was read hurriedly and then stowed away in the valise of the solicitor and the committee were not able to see it again. When I inquired for it of the clerk of the committee on the following day I found that it had never been handed in. I was under the impression that Mr. Ramsay was responsible in some way for the statement that an error had been made. I am surprised now to find, since I have received a copy of that letter and have had an opportunity of reading if carefully, that Mr. Ramsay makes no such statement. There is no evidence whether such a mistake was made in 1879. I am satisfied that no person could contend that. The solicitor of the company present at the Banking and Commerce Committee meeting, to the best of my recollection and I think I am right; and there are many hon. members who were present, could not get up and say that there was a mistake made. I have never found that any .such mistake was made in the legislation of 1879. I believe that Mr. Ramsay is the only living director at the present time, and I am surprised that this matter should have remained quiet so long until the men who knew all about it should have passed off the scene of action. I say advisedly that the committee was practically misled by the solicitor when he made the allegation that an error had occurred in the legislation of 1879 and that we were called upon to rectify that error. That was strongly impressed upon the committee and it very materially influenced the committee. A strong impression was made upon the committee that a mistake had been made in the legislation and that that mistake ought to be rectified. I am satisfied now, after having studied the whole question, that no mistake was made in tbe legislation of 1879, or yet in the preparation of the petition asking for that legislation. The matter having been pressed so strongly on the committee practically without evidence, but just on the statement of

the solicitor, I say that and that alone is a strong reason why the Bill should go back to the Committee on Banking and Commerce in order that they may deal with it more intelligently, knowing the facts now which they did not know before. I am strongly in favour of sending it back, however, that any interested party, be he policy-holder or whatever he may be, if he has an interest in this legislation, may be given an opportunity of stating his case. I could not conscientiously refuse any man that right. I can hardly believe that this House is going to refuse any policy-holder that right. The argument advanced by the hon: member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) that if it goes back to the Banking and Commerce Committee it will defeat the Bill for this session is not justified. Why should it be so? I think there is perhaps power enough behind the Throne to put this Bill through even if it does not go through to-night. I am not afraid but that there will be a way found of putting this Bill through after a week's or a few day's delay. Therefore, I do not think that the argument will have any force or weight with any hon. member. I know it will have no force or weight with me. I am going to do justice to the policyholders, although we have to delay the passing of the Bill for a whole week. I have many policy-holders in my own constituency. I am bound to protect their interests, and that practically is all the interest I have in it, because I am only a policyholder in the company for a very small sum. It is my duty as well to protect the policy-holders all over the country wherever they are. I propose to remain here for the purpose of doing that, and I hope and trust the House will see the propriety of adopting the motion proposed by my hon. friend from South Simeoe and of giving the people who are entitled to it the right to say whether they have a grievance or not before we undertake to deal finally with this Bill.

As a member of the Banking and Commerce Committee I desire to say that this Bill was discussed when it was before the committee and we considered that the notice had been properly given. I consider now that the notice, as printed in the Votes and Proceedings, was properly given in the first instance. If we sent the Bill back to the Banking and Commerce Committee, we would only quarrel over it for two or three days more and we would only arrive at the same conclusion that we arrived at the other day. I would not like the members of the House to be carried away by sensational statements about high salaries and the rights of policyholders. I represent a section of the country where, in proportion to its population there live as many policy-holders of the Canada Life as in any other section of Canada. The company has been well represented there for a great number of years and there are a great many policy-holders in the district. This agitation has been going on now for three months; it has been published in the papers, and the gentleman from Toronto who is at the back of it has been active. There was no discussion by the policy-holders before the Banking and Commerce Committee and the probability is that unless you go out and seek for it there will be no discussion there if the Bill is referred back. I was home for seven or eight days during the Easter recess and recently from Saturday morning until Sunday morning, and although the papers were full of this thing there was only one man among all the policy-holders in my section of the country who asked me anything about the Bill. He telphoned and asked me what it meant and I told him and he was perfectly satisfied. I am sorry to have to say it, but it is true, that many of the statements that have been made here tonight are pure sensationalism. There must be some reason for the opposition that does not appear on the surface because what the Canada Life asks in this Bill is to do what every insurance company doing business on the stock principle in Canada is doing to-day. I state here that the Canada Life Company has paid as good profits ever since its inception as any company doing business in Canada. That is a broad statement but I challenge any man to get up on the floor of this House and deny it, and if he does I can prove the truth of my statement. I think it would be ridiculous to send this Bill back to the Banking and Commerce Committee to have a reiteration of the same discussion that was carried on for two days already in that committee.
House divided on the amendment. (Mr. Lennox).

On the order for the consideration of Bill (No. 56) respecting the Canada Life Assurance Company.-Mr. A. H. Clarke.

I submit that we ought not to go on with this Bill at this hour of the night. It is a very important Bill, the merits of which have not been discussed at all on this side of the House. It is a Bill that is vital to the interest of 40,000 policy-holders-, representing about 200,000 people. We have been sitting here almost continuously since eleven o'clock this morning, it is now past twelve o clock, we must meet again at eleven, some of us have work at ten, and it is not fair to ask us to take up this Bill at this hour of the night. If the government insists on going on, we will have to discuss it as well as we can. It will take some time. I submit to the First Minister that although we could probably clear the Order Paper of most of the other private Bills, we ought not to be asked to take up this Bill now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the sense of the House is certainly in favour of this Bill. I think my hon. friend will admit that. We do not want to press the matter unduly. My hon. friend says that he wants to have discussion of the Bill. If the Bill is not unfairly dealt with, we certainly will endeavour to meet his wishes; but if we want to have prorogation soon, the business of the House must be proceeded with, and as the House has decided in favour of this Bill, I think it ought to go on.

The probability is that the First Minister is right in saying that the sense of the House is in favour of the Bill, in the sense that the majority are inclined at present to put it through. It may be that our discussion of the matter will be ineffective; but we will not assume that for the present. There are a number of gentleman on this side of the House who feel that it will be their duty to discuss this matter somewhat fully. I do not think there is any desire to prolong the discussion beyond what is necessary. Speaking for myself, I will only say what I believe to be in the interests of the public; but the Prime Minister must recognize that although the majority may be in favour of the Bill, yet the minority have a right to have a reasonable opportunity of expressing their views as forcibly as they possibly can.

Might I suggest to the Prime Minister that there are a great many Private Bills on the Order Paper that ought to be put through, and these could be run through in a very few moments. There will be an hour for private Bills to-morrow evening, when Mr. Conmee's Bill and this Bill could be dealt with, and we can clear the Order Paper with the exception of these two Bills.
I do not care to give way to other Bills. There is no reason why a Bill that has been discussed as much as this has been should stand over.
I think better progress will be made with the Bill if it is allowed to stand over.

We on this side of the House want to do everything we can to bring the session to a close at the time stated; but my right hon. friend knows that if we get up a little fight, it might last all night, and we would make no progress.
I suggest to him to accept the suggestion on this side of the House to clear the Order Paper of the other Bills, and let the two Bills referred to stand over.

The very negativing of the motion just voted on has forced upon us on this side of the House the necessity of taking a great deal more care before we let this Bill pass. We have prevented the public at large from coming before the ordinary committee of the House to present their views, and therefore it devolves upon us to be all the more careful to say everything they could possibly have said before the committee. Personally, I feel it incumbent upon me to investigate this Bill very thoroughly on the floor of this House, seeing that we have prevented the ordinary public from going before the Banking and Commerce Committee. We will now have to take the whole responsibility and of necessity we must discuss it at greater length. More time will therefore be consumed than would otherwise be required, and I do not think that in the long run we will gain anything by proceeding to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I appeal to my hon. friends on the other side. I would not press the Bill unduly; it is not a government Bill, but it is in charge of a private member. If it were a government Bill I know the course I would take, but as it is not I cannot do anything.
I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Order.

If my hon. friend who has charge of this Bill desires to meet the 173
wishes of the House on both sides and does not want to sit until 6 o'clock in the morning, he will consent to have this Bill stand. We have an hour for private Bills tomorrow night, when the leader of the opposition will be here, and then it can come up again on Friday night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Can we conclude this Bill on Friday?
I will not say that, but the leader of the opposition will be here then and there will be a better chance of concluding it if we do not get into any trouble over it.
If it goes over until Monday the Senate will have no time to discuss it.
They will have a week and a half. Our friends on this side are as anxious to conclude the session as hon. gentlemen opposite, but unless this course is adopted we will not get through on the 19th.
M^e don t care.

We don't care on this side either; I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
I think it is unreasonable to press the Bill now. I appeal to the Prime Minister to prevail on his friends to accept this reasonable proposition, clear the Order Paper of all these Bills, some of which are important, and let them go to the Senate. This Bill should not delay all the others, and it is not reasonable to expect members to remain here from 11 in the morning until after 12 at night. We have not yet made a start on this Bill and the chances are we will not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I want to be reasonable also. This is not a government Bill but a private Bill, and the promoter of the Bill is the best judge of his own interests. If my hon. friend were to accede to the suggestion I made that we could dispose of this Bill during the present week, I would advise my hon. friend to agree to that, but I am met with a negative. If hon. gentlemen would say that we will dispose of it this week, I would advise my hon. friend (Mr. A. H. Clarke) to agree.

I think the Prime Minister should be content to accept the assurance of members on this side that we have no desire to delay the Bill beyond a reasonable and fair discussion, and in all human probability it seems to me most likely it would get through this week, at the latest it will certainly get through next Monday. If the leader of the House would exercise his influence over one of his followers there would be little difficulty in controlling him to the extent of having the Bill delayed to-night



If, on the other hand, it is forced on against the wish of a large number of members who desire to have rest and to assist the leader of the House in closing the session, the experience of the past has been that we do not under such circumstances make the headway we ought.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend and I are old parliamentarians and we know that we can make progress and dispose of a matter in an hour's time or we can consume a great deal of time without making any progress. If he will say that the Bill will be put through this week I would say to agree.
On Friday night there will be an hour. If we do not finish tomorrow with a motion to complete the private Bills on Friday night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Very good, we will do that.

You might take all Friday night.
Progress reported.,

House in committee on Bill (No. 91) to incorporate the Prudential Trust Company. -Mr. Macdonell.
This is a contentious Bill, and I would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

It appears that only Bills are allowed to go through which stand in the name of the hon. gentlemen on the other side. This is the second Bill from this side which is objected to. We ought to know where we stand. Both can play that game. We came to an understanding to clear the paper provided the Canada Life Bill were held over. But now it seems that that understanding is not to apply to Bills from this side of the House. Bills standing in the name of supporters of the government are to pass, but those promoted by members of the opposition are to stand. We are certainly not going to submit to that sort of thing.

This is a Bill incorporating a trust company. So far as I am concerned, I am opposed to it, and I do not feel disposed to discuss it at this late hour.
I was not aware that it was the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) who was promoting this Bill, and I am objecting to it on that account.
What is your objection?

This Bill was before the Banking and Commerce Committee and was referred to a special committee and is probably the most contentious Bill that has come before a committee this session. Some of us have to meet at ten o'clock tomorrow morning for other business, and it Seems too bad that we should have to take up a contentious Bill.
Mr, LANCASTER. Some fifteen or twenty minutes ago the hon. gentleman was one of those who sang out the most loudly to rush through the Canada Life Bill.
What were you saying ten minutes ago?

I was saying that we should not deprive the policy-holders in the Canada Life of an opportunity of being heard against the Bill. But in the present, case there can be no objection of that kind. This Bill was thrashed out in

committee and all heard. The hon. member from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) does not want to deal with this Bill to-night. Well, we shall play the game all along the line. The hon. gentleman is breaking the arrangement made with the Prime Minister.

We came to an understanding with the Prime Minister that every Bill on the Order Paper was to be cleared except the Canada Life. If any hon. gentleman was not content with the arrangement he should have said so at the time. If we are not to be kept faith with, we shall know what to do. We have passed several Bills on that clear understanding, and it is absolutely unfair that the hon. member for Rainy River should act as he is doing. He first took objection to the Bill in the name of the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Smith). This hon. gentleman who is so anxious to get his own Bill through moves that the committee rise. Then we come to another Bill, we do not know who is promoting it. Does the Prime Minister think we are going down through all the other Bills after that? We are going to do nothing of the kind.

speechtext:
My hon.
friend puts the case in a manner which is not warranted by the facts. I suggested 'to the promoter of the Canada Life to postpone it until Friday evening, and to allow the Order Paper to be proceeded with. That does not mean that every Bill on the Order Paper must be taken up.

The proposition was not made by the First Minister, m so many Words, to clear the Order Paper; but the proposition of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) was that we should proceed and clear the Order Paper, and that was assented to so far as silence could give eon-feant, and I presumed that was the understanding. The leader of the government did not express dissent, nor was any dissent expressed by any member of the House. If these Bills require considerable discussion, I can see a good reason why they should stand over.

Personally I think it is a good reason, when the chairman of such an important committee tells us this is a contentious Bill, and the promoter is absent as well, that it should stand over. Now, my hoh. friend has asked on several occasions, when the promoter was absent, that we should not proceed with the Bill.
